title: Write the offer as a full package, not just a discount
hypothesis: If we write the offer in 5 parts (position, price, value mechanic, risk reversal, urgency) before launch, then conversion moves because buyers see a full package instead of a bare price cut.

signal.check: The current offer is stated only as a percent off or a price, with no written value mechanic or risk reversal.

risk.note: Low risk. This is a planning step and does not change price.

prerequisites: Current price and terms for the product written down
steps: Write the price and terms the buyer sees today.
Write the value mechanic: what the offer gives beyond the price.
Write the risk reversal: the guarantee or return terms.
Write the urgency element only if it is real and provable.
Check the ad, page and checkout say the same 5 parts.

test.method: Publish the rewritten offer with the same creative and traffic, and compare conversion before and after.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 100 orders on the new offer, whichever comes first

title: Name whether an offer targets conversion, basket size or repeat purchase
hypothesis: If we name which 1 of 3 things a margin trade targets (conversion, AOV or LTV) and model the downstream chain before launch, then we stop wasting margin because the offer is judged on the metric it was built to move.

signal.check: An offer or discount is live with no stated target metric and no CVR, AOV or LTV model behind it.

risk.note: Planning step; no price change.

prerequisites: List of every live offer and discount
steps: List every live offer: discounts, free shipping, gifts, email codes.
Name which 1 of 3 things each targets: conversion, basket size or repeat purchase.
Model the downstream chain: CVR, AOV, CAC, ROAS, contribution, LTV.
Drop or rebuild any offer with no clear target.

test.method: Track the named metric for each offer for one full cycle and compare it to the offer's stated target.
test.measure: cvr_overall, aov or ltv_180d, matched to the offer's stated target
test.read_point: After one full order cycle, 30 to 90 days depending on the repeat cycle

title: Score the product offer against the value equation before cutting price
hypothesis: If we score dream outcome, likelihood, time delay and effort for the offer against a real competitor, then conversion moves because we fix the weakest driver instead of only cutting price.

signal.check: Nobody has scored the product's outcome, proof, delivery speed and checkout effort against a real competitor.

risk.note: Scoring exercise only; no live change is required to do it.

prerequisites: A named buyer avatar for the product
A visible competitor selling a similar product
steps: Pick 1 product and 1 buyer avatar.
Score likelihood: count readable reviews, check for a demo or unboxing video.
Score time delay: record delivery speed and any stated delivery date.
Score effort: walk mobile checkout for friction.
Give each driver a 0 or 1 against the strongest competitor.
Fix the driver that scores 0 first, before raising any claim.

test.method: Re-score the same product after fixes ship and compare to the baseline score.
test.read_point: After the fixes ship and 2 weeks of traffic pass

title: Fix each value-equation driver with its own lever
hypothesis: If we name the dream outcome, add proof, shorten delivery time and cut checkout effort, then conversion rises because each driver of buyer value gets a concrete fix instead of a vague claim.

signal.check: The PDP names only the product category, has no demo or unboxing content, ships in 2 weeks or more, or forces account creation at checkout.

risk.note: Copy and checkout changes are reversible; test before a full rollout.

prerequisites: A value equation score from a prior audit, or a fresh one
steps: Name the end state the buyer wants, not the category, in the headline.
Add a demo or unboxing video, plus readable reviews, as proof.
State a real delivery date or shorten dispatch time.
Add express wallets, guest checkout and how-to content to cut effort.
Ship the cheapest fixes first.

test.method: Run an A/B or before-after test of the PDP and checkout changes on the same traffic.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or the sample size 09-CRO sets

title: Show a real product improvement on the page once it exists
hypothesis: If we show a real product or service improvement on the page instead of assuming buyers notice it, then conversion moves because perceived value only counts what is visible.

signal.check: A real improvement was made in the last 90 days but the page copy still describes the old version.

risk.note: Copy change only.

prerequisites: A list of real, recent product or service improvements
steps: List every real improvement made in the last 90 days.
Add each one to the PDP, ad or email before the buyer decides.
Remove any improvement claim that is not true today.

test.method: Compare conversion on the updated page against the prior version.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks of traffic on the updated page

title: Differentiate a commodity SKU's offer instead of cutting its price
hypothesis: If we rebuild the package (bundle, kit, guarantee, bonus or name) for a commodity SKU instead of cutting price, then margin holds because buyers stop comparing on price alone.
does_not_apply_when: The product is genuinely undifferentiated and there is no room to add a bundle, kit, guarantee or bonus

signal.check: Reviews, support or chat repeat that the product is the same as a cheaper option and buyers ask for a price match.

risk.note: A weak repackaging can look like a price hike in disguise; keep the underlying price stable while testing.

prerequisites: Objection list from reviews and support showing price-comparison language
steps: Confirm the objection is price comparison, not a real quality gap.
Build a bundle, kit, guarantee or bonus a bare price match cannot copy.
Rename or reposition the offer around that package.
Test the repackaged offer against the current one.

test.method: Run the repackaged offer against the current one on equal traffic.
test.read_point: After the sample size 09-CRO sets for the test

title: Match the ad's offer to the landing page and checkout
hypothesis: If the desire, proof, delivery promise, risk reversal and price in the ad match the landing page, then conversion rises because buyers do not feel misled between click and purchase.

signal.check: The ad promises a price, gift or guarantee that the landing page does not show, or shows differently.

risk.note: Copy alignment only.

prerequisites: Access to the live ad and its landing page for the same offer
steps: List the desire, proof, delivery promise, risk reversal and price shown in the ad.
Check the landing page states the same 5 things.
Fix any mismatch on the page, not the ad, unless the ad overstates the offer.

test.method: Compare landing page conversion before and after the match is fixed, on the same ad traffic.
test.read_point: After 1 to 2 weeks of matched ad traffic

title: Build the offer around the buyer's single biggest objection
hypothesis: If the offer's guarantee, bonus or bundle answers the buyer's single biggest objection, then conversion rises because the offer removes the real reason people do not buy.

signal.check: No objection list exists from reviews, support tickets, chat logs or cancel reasons.

risk.note: Requires only research and offer wording changes.

prerequisites: Objection list from reviews, support, chat or cancel reasons
steps: Pull the objection list from reviews, support tickets, chat and cancel reasons.
Rank objections by how often they appear.
Build the guarantee, bonus or bundle piece that answers the top objection.
Put that piece in the offer's headline or buy box, not buried in the FAQ.

test.method: Compare conversion before and after the objection-led offer piece ships.

title: Reposition a hero SKU into several offers by persona
hypothesis: If the same hero SKU is offered under different persona-led angles with dedicated pages, then conversion and reach both grow because the SKU serves several jobs without new inventory or margin cost.

signal.check: The brand sells 1 hero SKU with 1 generic page and angle, but reviews or support show several different reasons people buy it.

risk.note: More pages to maintain; any health or outcome angle needs a claims check.

prerequisites: List of jobs or personas the SKU serves
Ability to test angles as ads
steps: List the different jobs or personas the SKU serves.
Test each job as a distinct ad angle.
Build a dedicated page and offer for each angle that gets real traction.
Keep the SKU and price the same across pages; only positioning changes.
Add a claims check before any health or outcome angle goes live.

test.method: Run each angle as its own ad set and dedicated page, and compare conversion and CAC by angle.
test.read_point: After each angle gets enough spend for a read, per 09-CRO

title: Map the product use journey to find bundle and bonus ideas
hypothesis: If we map what the buyer must do before, during and after using the product, then we surface bundle and bonus ideas because each friction point points to a component that removes it.

signal.check: The offer has no bonus or add-on beyond the core product, and nobody has mapped before, during and after use.

risk.note: A research step; no live change on its own.

prerequisites: Access to reviews, support tickets and usage questions
steps: List what the buyer must do before using the product (setup, decision, unboxing).
List what they must do during use (dosing, storage, maintenance).
List what they must do after use (disposal, refill, next purchase).
Turn each friction point into a candidate bundle item or bonus.
Shortlist only items that are cheap to the brand or free.

test.method: Cost and test the top candidate items with the bundle or gift procedure before adding them.
test.read_point: After the bundle or bonus ships and 1 order cycle passes

title: Cut offer components buyers do not value after 90 to 120 days
hypothesis: If we survey buyers after 90 to 120 days and remove offer components nobody valued, then margin improves because the brand stops paying for parts that do not change the decision.

signal.check: The offer stacks several bonuses, gifts or guarantees, and nobody has checked which ones buyers actually noticed or used.

risk.note: Removing a low-value component is low risk if buyers are surveyed first.

prerequisites: An offer that has been live for 90 to 120 days
Ability to survey recent buyers
steps: Survey recent buyers on which offer parts convinced them or which they used.
Rank the parts by how many buyers noticed or valued them.
Remove the lowest-value, highest-cost parts first.
Watch take rate and conversion after the cut.

test.method: Compare conversion and margin before and after removing the low-value component.
test.read_point: After 1 order cycle following the cut

title: Check market and product fit before spending on offer tests
hypothesis: If we confirm the category is not shrinking and the product genuinely repeats before testing offers, then wasted test spend falls because no offer fixes a bad market or product fit.

signal.check: Offer tests are planned or running while nobody has checked category growth or the product's real repeat rate.

risk.note: A check, not a live change.

prerequisites: Category growth data or trend
Product's real repeat-purchase rate
steps: Check whether the product category is growing or shrinking.
Check the product's real repeat rate, not an assumed one.
If the category is shrinking or the product does not repeat, fix that before testing offers.
Only start offer testing once market and product fit are confirmed.

test.method: Run this as a gate before any offer test plan is approved, not as a live test.
test.read_point: Before any offer test budget is committed

title: Route marketplace deal mechanics to the marketplace and ad playbooks
hypothesis: If marketplace-specific deal mechanics (coupons, Lightning Deals, Subscribe and Save) are built in the marketplace and ad playbooks instead of here, then the offer stays correct because platform fees and rules are handled where they are tracked.

signal.check: A marketplace-heavy brand is planning a coupon, lightning deal or subscribe-and-save mechanic inside the general offer plan instead of the marketplace playbook.

risk.note: A routing decision, not a live change.

prerequisites: Confirmed marketplace_heavy store tag
steps: Confirm the brand sells on a marketplace with its own deal mechanics.
Route coupon, Lightning Deal and Subscribe and Save design to the marketplace and ad playbooks.
Keep only the outcome-word search-term naming step here.

test.method: Not applicable; this is a routing decision, reviewed whenever a new marketplace deal is planned.
test.read_point: Reviewed whenever a new marketplace deal is planned

title: Build the full margin waterfall for every SKU before any offer
hypothesis: If we compute price, all-in COGS, shipping, fulfilment, fees, gross margin and break-even ROAS for every SKU, then every later offer decision improves because it is judged against a real baseline instead of a guess.

signal.check: No per-SKU gross margin, break-even ROAS or target CPA exists, or COGS excludes shipping and fees.

risk.note: A calculation step; no live change.

prerequisites: Price list per SKU
All-in COGS per SKU
Shipping cost by units per order
Payment and app fees per order
steps: Pull price, all-in COGS, shipping cost for 1 to 6 units, fulfilment cost and fees per SKU.
Compute gross margin per order and gross margin percent in code.
Compute break-even ROAS and target CPA in code.
Pull 90 to 180 days of sessions, orders, CVR, order values and units per order.
Mark any missing input as unavailable and request it, instead of guessing.

test.method: Not a live test; a one-time and then quarterly recompute of the waterfall.
test.read_point: Before any offer is proposed, and after any price or cost change

title: Judge every offer on contribution per order and per visitor, not revenue or ROAS
hypothesis: If we compare offers on contribution per order and per visitor instead of revenue, ROAS, AOV or take rate, then we stop shipping offers that look good but lose money.

signal.check: Offer decisions are being made on ROAS, revenue or AOV alone, with no contribution-per-order or per-visitor figure attached.

risk.note: A reporting change, not a live change.

prerequisites: Gross margin waterfall from OFF-014
steps: Compute contribution per order (gross margin minus CAC) for the current and any proposed offer.
Compute contribution per visitor (CVR times gross margin, minus ad spend per session).
Add both figures to every offer comparison, next to revenue and ROAS.
Reject any offer that raises revenue or ROAS but lowers contribution per visitor.

test.method: Recompute contribution per order and per visitor whenever 2 offers are compared.
test.measure: contribution_margin per order and per visitor

title: Reset target ROAS and CPA whenever the offer structure changes
hypothesis: If we recompute target ROAS and CPA every time a bundle, gift or free unit changes the margin structure, then paid spend stays profitable because the paid team is never buying against stale targets.

signal.check: An offer's tier depth, gifts or free units changed recently but the paid team's target ROAS or CPA has not been updated.

risk.note: Stale targets can quietly burn margin until caught.

prerequisites: Gross margin waterfall from OFF-014
steps: Recompute gross margin per order for the new offer structure.
Recompute break-even ROAS and target CPA from the new margin.
Hand the new targets to the paid team in writing.
Confirm the paid platform's bid or budget rules reflect the new target.

test.method: Compare achieved ROAS against the new target for 1 to 2 weeks after the change.
test.read_point: 1 to 2 weeks after any offer structure change

title: Model discount depth on units per order, not on an assumed lift
hypothesis: If we model a discount's new AOV from a real units-per-transaction lift and apply COGS to full retail units, then the discount's true margin impact is known because neither the lift nor the cost is guessed.

signal.check: A discount is modelled with COGS applied to the discounted price, or with an assumed units-per-order lift that was never measured.

risk.note: A calculation fix; catches an overstated margin before launch.

prerequisites: Past sale periods with units-per-order data, or a conservative fallback of no lift
steps: Pull units per transaction from past sale periods at a similar depth.
If no history exists, use the current units per order as the conservative case.
Apply COGS percent to the full retail unit price, not the discounted price.
Recompute new AOV, COGS, shipping and gross margin from these inputs.

test.method: Compare the modelled margin against the actual margin after the discount runs.

title: Check how fast required ROAS rises before approving a deeper discount
hypothesis: If we compute required ROAS at each discount depth before approving it, then we avoid discounts the brand cannot pay for because required ROAS rises much faster than break-even ROAS as margin thins.

signal.check: A discount depth is being considered with no computed required ROAS, only a break-even ROAS check.

risk.note: A calculation check, not a live change.

prerequisites: Gross margin waterfall from OFF-014
Current target ROAS
steps: Compute allowable CAC and required ROAS at the proposed discount depth.
Compute the efficiency lift needed versus the current target ROAS.
Compare that lift to the brand's own measured sale-period lift.
Reject the depth if it needs a lift the brand has never achieved.

test.method: Track achieved ROAS against the required ROAS for the approved depth.
test.read_point: During and after the discount period

title: Measure the brand's own sale-period efficiency lift before trusting a discount
hypothesis: If we measure ROAS or CPA in the brand's own past sale periods versus non-sale periods, then discount planning improves because efficiency lift is brand-specific and can range from about 5% to 80%.

signal.check: No comparison exists between the brand's ROAS or CPA in past sale periods and non-sale periods.

expected_effect.size: 70% to 80% for rare discounters, about 5% for known discounters (source range, not this brand's number)

risk.note: A measurement step.

prerequisites: Past sale period dates, depth, ROAS or CPA, and units per order
steps: List every past sale period with its dates and depth.
Pull ROAS or CPA for each sale period and the non-sale periods around it.
Compute the efficiency lift the brand actually got.
Use this measured lift, not a source's number, in every future discount model.
If no sale history exists, assume the low end of the range.

test.method: Recompute the measured lift after each new sale period to refine the number.

title: Match how aggressive an offer's first-order loss is to real cash on hand
hypothesis: If we size any first-order loss (a discounted or loss-leading subscription order) against months of cash runway and proven payback, then the brand avoids running out of cash on an offer it cannot fund.

signal.check: A subscription or bundle offer that loses money on order 1 is running or planned with no stated cash runway or payback check.

risk.note: Running a funded loss without cash to back it can force a sudden stop mid-cohort.

prerequisites: Cash on hand
Monthly ad spend
Months to payback from 20-FIN
steps: Get cash on hand, monthly ad spend and months to payback.
Classify the brand as cash-tight, funded or aggressive.
Cash-tight: only run offers profitable on order 1.
Funded: allow a first-order loss only with proven cohort LTGP and payback.
Aggressive: allow a bigger loss only with reserves to cover several months.

test.method: Track cash runway monthly against the offer's modelled payback period.
test.read_point: Monthly, and before scaling spend on any loss-leading offer

title: Fix basket structure before spending more on ads for a low-AOV hero SKU
hypothesis: If a single hero SKU cannot cover its CAC, then building a multi-pack or bundle before raising ad spend improves profit because a $14 to $25 CAC cannot sit on a $14 order.

signal.check: The store sells 1 low-price hero SKU as a single unit and its contribution per order is negative or near 0 at the current blended CAC.

risk.note: Building a pack takes packaging and inventory changes before it can launch.

prerequisites: Blended CAC or CPA
AOV and gross margin for the single-unit offer
steps: Compute contribution per order for the current single-unit offer at the blended CAC.
If it is negative or near 0, stop increasing ad spend on that offer.
Build a multi-pack or bundle ladder (see the bundle ladder ideas) before spending more.
Recompute contribution per order for the new pack before scaling spend again.

test.method: Compare contribution per order for the single unit versus the new pack, at the same CAC.
test.read_point: Before increasing ad spend, and again after the pack launches

title: Use the AOV times CVR screen only as a first sort, then run full economics
hypothesis: If we use AOV times CVR as a first pass filter and always follow it with a full contribution model, then weak offers get filtered fast without being wrongly approved on a screen that ignores margin.

signal.check: An offer idea is being ranked or rejected using only the AOV times CVR screen, with no margin or contribution model after it.

risk.note: A screening step only; must not replace the full margin model.

prerequisites: AOV, CVR and currency for the brand
steps: Convert the screen's threshold to the brand's own currency and price level.
Compute AOV times CVR (as a plain number, not a percent) for each candidate offer.
Use it only to sort candidates, pass or fail.
Run the full contribution-per-order and per-visitor model on every candidate next.

test.method: Not a live test; a filtering step run before deeper offer costing.
test.read_point: Whenever a new offer idea is screened

title: Judge offer tests on gross profit and a repeat-cycle LTV window, not first-order results
hypothesis: If we judge an offer test on gross profit and LTV at the product's repeat-purchase window instead of first-order results, then we avoid keeping an offer that wins order 1 but lowers repeat purchase.

signal.check: An offer test was declared a winner using only first-order revenue, AOV or conversion, before any repeat-purchase data came in.

risk.note: A measurement discipline change, not a live product change.

prerequisites: A defined repeat-purchase cycle length for the product
steps: Set the test's read window to the product's repeat-purchase cycle, not an arbitrary date.
Track gross profit per order for each arm through that window.
Track LTV or repeat rate for each arm's buyers through that window.
Only declare a winner once the LTV read is in, not on day 1 results.

test.method: Hold the test open through the full repeat-cycle window before declaring a winner.
test.read_point: At the end of the product's repeat-purchase cycle

title: Add value before cutting price
hypothesis: If we widen the gap between value and price by adding value (a bonus, a guarantee, a bundle) instead of cutting price, then margin holds because price can only fall to 0 while value can keep rising.

signal.check: The default response to a slow SKU or a stalled offer is to plan a price cut, before any value addition has been tried.

risk.note: Value additions are easier to remove later than a price cut is to reverse.

prerequisites: A specific SKU or offer flagged as underperforming
steps: List 2 to 3 value additions (bonus, guarantee, bundle, gift) that cost little to the brand.
Test 1 value addition against the current price before testing a price cut.
Only consider a modelled markdown if value additions do not move conversion.

test.method: Run the value-added offer against the current offer on equal traffic.

title: Match a competitor or marketplace price only when landed cost supports it
hypothesis: If we match a competitor or marketplace price only when our landed cost per unit is close to a fraction of theirs, then margin holds because we do not chase a price a thinner cost structure can absorb and ours cannot.

signal.check: Pressure exists to match a competitor's or a marketplace's listed price with no landed-cost comparison done first.

risk.note: Matching price without checking cost can turn every matched order into a loss.

prerequisites: Landed cost per unit
A comparable competitor or marketplace price
steps: Get the brand's own landed cost per unit for the SKU.
Estimate or find the competitor's landed cost, or use the price gap as a proxy.
Match the price only if the brand's landed cost is low enough to absorb it.
Route marketplace price-parity SKUs to 12-GAD for shopping-feed rules.

test.method: Track gross margin per order on matched-price SKUs after the match.
test.read_point: After 1 month of the matched price live

title: Test a higher price with a positioning change instead of only lowering price
hypothesis: If a low headline price reads as low quality, then testing a higher price alongside a positioning change (audience, hero image, bundle) can lift sales because price alone was never the only signal buyers used.

signal.check: A SKU is priced at the bottom of its category and conversion is still weak, with no positioning test tried before further discounting.

risk.note: A price rise without a real positioning change can just lose sales; test both together.

prerequisites: A PDP that can be duplicated or A/B tested
steps: Pick 1 underperforming, low-priced SKU.
Change positioning: hero image, audience framing or a bundle, at the same time as a price rise.
Run the new price and positioning against the old one on equal traffic.
Read conversion and contribution together, not price alone.

test.method: A/B test the repositioned, higher-priced PDP against the original.

title: Cut flat, frequent discounting that trains buyers to wait
hypothesis: If we reduce the frequency of flat sitewide discounts, then full-price revenue share rises because frequent discounting re-anchors price and trains repeat buyers to wait for the next sale.

signal.check: Discount share of revenue is high and a meaningful share of repeat buyers only purchase during a sale.

risk.note: Cutting discount frequency can dip short-term revenue before full-price demand recovers.

prerequisites: Discount share of revenue
Share of repeat buyers who only buy on sale
steps: Measure discount share of revenue and the share of repeat buyers who only buy on sale.
Set a cap on flat sitewide sales per year (start from the brand's own history).
Replace some flat discounts with an evergreen stacked offer instead.
Track full-price revenue share for 30 days after each change.

test.method: Compare discount share of revenue and full-price share before and after the frequency cut.

title: Never show a reference price or bonus value that is not real
hypothesis: If every was-price, up-to-savings claim and stated bonus value is a real, recent, provable price, then legal and trust risk falls because no claim can be shown to be invented.

signal.check: A strike-through was-price, an up-to-X-off claim, or a stated bonus value is live and nobody can point to when that higher price or value was actually charged.

risk.note: An invented reference price is a dark-pattern and consumer-law risk in several countries.

prerequisites: Selling countries confirmed
Price history for any SKU with a was-price claim
steps: List every was-price, up-to-X-off claim and stated bonus value live on any surface.
For each, find the real, recent price or sale record that supports it.
Remove or fix any claim that cannot be supported.
Flag every remaining claim for a web check on reference-price rules by selling country.

test.method: Not a live test; a compliance audit run before launch and periodically after.
test.read_point: Before any launch and every 6 months

title: Always show the full price next to any per-day or per-unit figure
hypothesis: If the total price is always shown next to any per-day or per-serving figure, then trust and compliance both hold because a per-day number never hides what the buyer actually pays.

signal.check: A per-day, per-serving or first-instalment number appears on the page or in an ad without the full total price next to it.

risk.note: Drip pricing without a visible total is a regulatory risk in several markets.

prerequisites: List of every surface showing a per-day, per-serving or instalment figure
steps: Find every place a per-day, per-serving or instalment number is shown.
Add the full total price next to each one, not instead of it.
Flag instalment or BNPL disclosure for a web check by country.

test.method: Not a live test; a page and ad copy audit.
test.read_point: Before launch and after any pricing display change

title: Notify subscribers and update every channel before a real price rise
hypothesis: If active subscribers and cart abandoners are notified and every ad and PDP is updated before a real price rise takes effect, then trust holds because no channel shows a stale price at launch.

signal.check: A price increase is planned or was recently made with no subscriber notice and no check of live ads and PDPs for the old price.

risk.note: A price rise is hard to walk back once subscribers are billed at the new rate; get the rollout right first.

prerequisites: The new price is real and dated
steps: Confirm the new price is real, dated and finalised.
Notify active subscribers and recent cart abandoners before it goes live.
Update every running ad and every PDP to the new price at the same time.
Check no channel still shows the old price after launch.

test.method: Crawl every live ad and PDP right after the price change to confirm consistency.
test.read_point: Within 24 hours of the price change going live

title: Give a discount only in exchange for a bigger order, a subscription, or clearing stock
hypothesis: If every discount is tied to a bigger order, a subscription signup, or clearing stuck stock, then margin holds because a flat discount on the hero product alone buys only a small, unpaid-for conversion bump.
does_not_apply_when: The brand is a fixed-offer brand; it gets presentation fixes, not new discounts

signal.check: A discount is live on a single SKU with no bigger-order, subscription or stock-clearance condition attached.

risk.note: Removing an unconditional discount can dip short-term conversion until the conditional offer replaces it.

prerequisites: Current live discounts listed with their conditions, if any
steps: List every live discount and whether it has a condition attached.
Attach each unconditional discount to a bigger order, a subscription, or clearance stock.
Remove any flat discount that trades margin for nothing in return.

test.method: Compare units per order and contribution per order before and after adding the condition.
test.read_point: After 1 order cycle on the conditional offer

title: Limit flat discounts to 1 or 2 times a year, on high-margin SKUs or clearance stock only
hypothesis: If flat, sitewide discounts are capped to 1 or 2 times a year and used only on a few high-margin SKUs or clearance stock, then price integrity holds because the discount is never used to rescue a revenue number.

signal.check: Flat sitewide discounts have run more than twice in the last 12 months, or one is being planned to hit a revenue target.

risk.note: A policy change; enforce it before the next planned sale.

prerequisites: Count of flat sitewide sales run in the last 12 months
steps: Count flat sitewide discounts run in the last 12 months.
Set a written cap of 1 to 2 a year going forward.
Reserve any flat discount for a few very high-margin SKUs or grade-C clearance stock.
Decline any request to discount only to hit a revenue number.

test.method: Track flat discount count and discount share of revenue over the next 12 months.

title: Find the profit-maximising discount depth from the brand's own sale history
hypothesis: If we plot contribution per order against discount depth from at least 3 past sale periods, then the next sale can be priced at the depth that peaks contribution instead of guessing.

signal.check: The brand has run flat discounts at 3 or more depths but nobody has plotted contribution per order against depth.

risk.note: An analysis step, run before the next sale is priced.

prerequisites: At least 3 past flat-discount periods at different depths, with units per order and contribution data
steps: Build a table of depth, units per order, average unit retail and contribution per order for past sales.
Plot contribution per order against depth.
Pick the depth at the peak, ruling out any depth the brand has never hit the required ROAS for.
If sale history is missing or messy, do not guess; propose a structural offer instead.
Treat price-ending or odd-number discount tests as low priority, run only after this depth is settled.

test.method: Run the next sale at the identified peak depth and compare its contribution per order to the plot's prediction.
test.read_point: After the next sale period closes

title: Choose dollar-off or percent-off framing based on AOV and currency
hypothesis: If we show a fixed currency saving above about the brand's own AOV threshold and a percent saving below it, then the discount reads bigger to buyers because the framing matches which number looks larger at that price point.
does_not_apply_when: The threshold is a USD heuristic and must be converted to the brand's own currency and price level before use

signal.check: Discounts are shown the same way (always percent, or always currency) regardless of the product's price point.

risk.note: A copy and framing change only.

prerequisites: The brand's typical AOV and selling currency
steps: Convert the AOV threshold to the brand's own currency.
For products above the threshold, show the discount as a currency amount.
For products below the threshold, show it as a percent.
Always show the larger of the 2 numbers, whichever framing is used.

test.method: A/B test currency versus percent framing on the same discount and traffic.

title: Frame extra free units as free, not as an equivalent percent off
hypothesis: If an extra unit at the same total price is framed as buy-2-get-1-free instead of an equivalent percent off, then conversion rises because free reads as a stronger offer at the identical price.
does_not_apply_when: The economics do not work: a free unit is real COGS and freight and must clear the tier's contribution target first

signal.check: A multi-unit discount is shown only as a percent off (for example 33% off 3) instead of a free-unit frame.

risk.note: A framing change; the underlying price and margin must stay identical.

prerequisites: Tier contribution check (F10) confirms the free unit clears the contribution target
steps: Confirm the free-unit tier clears its contribution target with the gift cost included.
State the correct percent equivalent (buy 2 get 1 free is 33.3% off 3, not 60% off).
Frame the tier copy as 'buy 2, get 1 free' rather than the percent.
Test the free-unit frame against the percent frame if unsure.

test.method: A/B test the free-unit frame against the percent-off frame at the same total price.

title: Test a free sample or usage credit against an equal-cost cash discount
hypothesis: If we test a free sample, extra unit or usage credit against an equal-cost cash discount, then we may find a lift because a tied-to-product benefit can beat cash at the same cost, though this is old direct-mail evidence and must be tested fresh.

signal.check: The brand only ever offers cash discounts and has never tested a same-cost product credit or sample against one.

risk.note: The underlying evidence is from 1992 to 2008 direct mail; treat the result as a test, not a fact.

prerequisites: A pop-up or win-back flow to run the test in
steps: Pick 1 surface to test: the pop-up or a win-back email.
Build a sample, extra unit or usage-credit arm at the same cost as the current cash discount.
Run both arms on equal traffic.
Read placed-order rate and gross profit, not opt-ins.

test.method: Run the credit or sample arm against the cash-discount arm on equal traffic.

title: Never make the buyer do mental math on a discount
hypothesis: If every discount label shows currency saved and per-unit or per-serving cost instead of an odd percent, then conversion improves because buyers do not have to calculate the real saving themselves.

signal.check: A tier or discount label reads like '67% off the 3rd unit' or another figure that does not describe the whole basket's real saving.

risk.note: A copy fix only.

prerequisites: List of every discount and tier label currently live
steps: List every discount or tier label live on the site and in ads.
Compute the real currency saved and per-unit or per-serving cost for each.
Rewrite any label that requires mental math to understand.
Check the new label against the 'no mental math' rule before publishing.

test.method: Compare conversion on the rewritten labels against the old ones.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks of traffic on the new labels

title: Give new and returning customers different offers
hypothesis: If new customers see a first-purchase offer and returning customers see a lock-in or larger-pack offer instead of the same sitewide discount, then repeat rate and margin both improve because retention offers stop training everyone to expect a discount.

signal.check: The same discount or offer is shown to new and returning customers on every surface.

risk.note: Requires audience segmentation on-site and in email or ads.

prerequisites: Ability to segment offers by new versus returning customer
steps: Segment the audience into new and returning customers on-site and in ads.
Build a first-purchase offer for new customers.
Build a lock-in, subscription or larger-pack offer for returning customers.
Stop showing the sitewide discount to the whole audience unconditionally.

test.method: Compare repeat rate and discount share of revenue before and after segmenting the offer.

title: Offer a prepaid discount or COD-fee waiver to shift a COD-heavy market to prepaid
hypothesis: If we offer a small prepaid discount or a cash-on-delivery fee waiver above a basket size, then prepaid share rises because a COD-heavy, mobile-first market gets a concrete reason to pay upfront.

signal.check: A large share of orders are cash on delivery in a market where COD is common, with no prepaid incentive offered.

risk.note: No source in this playbook backs this; verify against the brand's own COD share and RTO cost before running it.

prerequisites: COD share of orders
COD-related return-to-origin cost
steps: Measure the current COD share of orders and its return-to-origin cost.
Set a small prepaid discount or COD fee waiver above a basket size.
Launch it at checkout where COD is offered.
Track prepaid share and RTO cost for 30 days.

test.method: Compare prepaid share and RTO cost before and after the incentive launches.

title: Test discount structure changes before testing discount depth
hypothesis: If we change the offer's structure (gift versus credit versus bundle versus subscription terms) before testing different discount depths, then test results are more useful because a depth test alone does not count as an offer test.

signal.check: The only offer tests planned or run are different discount depths (10% vs 20% vs 30%), with no structural variant tested.

risk.note: A test-planning discipline, not a live change.

prerequisites: A test roadmap or backlog of offer ideas
steps: Review the test roadmap for depth-only tests (10% vs 20% vs 30%).
Replace or precede them with a structural test: gift vs credit vs bundle vs subscription terms.
Run the structural test first; only test depth once structure is settled.

test.method: Not a live test itself; a rule applied when building the test roadmap.
test.measure: cvr_overall and contribution_margin, by structural variant

title: Fund multi-pack pricing from shipping savings first, then margin
hypothesis: If the falling per-unit price in a quantity ladder comes from real shipping and fulfilment savings on bigger boxes first, then the ladder holds margin because the discount is funded by a real cost drop, not by giving up profit.

signal.check: A quantity ladder's per-unit price falls with size, but nobody has checked how much of that fall shipping and fulfilment actually pay for.

risk.note: A calculation input to ladder pricing, not a live change on its own.

prerequisites: Shipping and 3PL cost by units per order
steps: Get shipping and 3PL cost for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 units in a box.
Compute the per-unit shipping saving at each tier size.
Use that saving to fund the ladder's per-unit price fall first.
Only dip into product margin if shipping savings are not enough for a meaningful tier gap.

test.method: Compare modelled versus actual per-order margin once the ladder is live.
test.read_point: After 1 order cycle on the new ladder

title: Build a buy-more-save-more ladder for a consumable or multi-unit product
hypothesis: If we launch a 3-tier buy-more-save-more ladder for a consumable or multi-unit product, then AOV rises because the ladder adds real value, filters out pure discount hunters, and anchors the middle tier as the natural choice.
does_not_apply_when: The product has no real reason to own more than 1 at a time, or inventory cannot support the top tier

signal.check: The product is shelf-stable or used repeatedly, but is only sold as a single unit with no quantity ladder.

risk.note: Requires inventory to support the top tier and packaging or listing changes.

prerequisites: Confirmed shelf-stable or repeat-use product
Inventory to support the top tier
steps: Confirm the product is shelf-stable, multi-unit, and has a real reason to own more than 1.
Choose quantities: for example 1, 2, 3 or 1, 3, 6.
Price so per-unit price falls with quantity, funded by shipping savings first.
Launch and track take rate by tier.

test.method: Compare AOV and take rate by tier before and after the ladder launches.

title: Bundle the same product or a true routine, not a forced mixed assortment
hypothesis: If bundles use the same product (more units, flavours or colours) or items that form a real routine, then take rate holds because buyers are not forced to take 2 of 3 items they do not want.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has 1 non-consumable hero product with genuinely related accessories, where a mixed bundle can work

signal.check: A live bundle forces together unrelated products the buyer may only want some of.

risk.note: Rebuilding a bundle's contents is reversible.

prerequisites: Current bundle contents and their individual take rates, if known
steps: List current bundles and whether their items form a real routine.
Rebuild any forced mixed bundle into a same-SKU or true-routine bundle.
Test the rebuilt bundle against the old one where possible.

test.method: Compare take rate and return rate of the rebuilt bundle against the old one.

title: Use 3 tiers with the middle one pre-selected as the default
hypothesis: If a quantity or plan ladder shows 3 tiers with the middle one pre-selected, then take rate on that tier rises because the default bias decides most buyers' choice.
does_not_apply_when: Return rate by tier shows a larger default raises returns in a fit-sensitive category

signal.check: A ladder or plan selector defaults to the smallest or largest option instead of the middle.

risk.note: A default-selection change; verify the platform's widget supports it.

prerequisites: A ladder or plan selector that supports a default option (verify UI)
steps: Confirm the tier or plan the brand wants to sell most (based on contribution, not just size).
Set that tier as the pre-selected default in the buy box.
Keep the single or smallest option at full price as the anchor.

test.method: Compare take rate by tier before and after changing the default.

title: Step the per-unit price down with each ladder tier
hypothesis: If per-unit price falls with each higher tier in the ladder, then the top tier has a real reason to exist because buyers can see the deal getting better as they buy more.

signal.check: The per-unit price is flat or barely falls between tiers, so the biggest tier offers no extra saving.

risk.note: A pricing recalculation.

prerequisites: Per-unit price and cost at each existing tier
steps: Compute per-unit price at each existing tier.
Confirm it falls meaningfully at each step up.
Reprice any tier where per-unit price is flat or barely falls.

test.method: Compare tier take rate before and after repricing so per-unit price clearly falls.

title: Keep a low-friction, full-price entry tier in every ladder
hypothesis: If the smallest ladder tier stays at full price as the entry option, then overall conversion and profit per customer hold because buyers are not forced into only a large-pack purchase.

signal.check: The only option on a product page is the largest pack, with no single-unit or smallest option available.

risk.note: Adding back a smaller option is low risk.

prerequisites: Ability to sell the product as a single unit
steps: Check whether a single-unit, full-price option exists on the page.
Add it back if it does not, and keep it at full price as the anchor.
Keep the middle tier as the pre-selected default, not the entry tier.

test.method: Compare conversion and AOV before and after the entry tier is restored.

title: Give every ladder tier a real physical reason to exist
hypothesis: If each tier is labelled with a real reason (coverage, room size, days of supply, family size) instead of only 'save more', then take rate improves because buyers can match the tier to their own need.

signal.check: Ladder tiers are labelled only by quantity and percent saved, with no stated reason to pick one over another.

risk.note: A copy change only.

prerequisites: Real usage data: coverage area, days of supply, or household size per unit
steps: Work out the real usage reason for each tier (days of supply, coverage, household size).
Write a short reason label for each tier.
Replace 'save more' style labels with the reason-based ones.

test.method: Compare tier take rate before and after adding reason labels.

title: Put the variant selector above the quantity ladder
hypothesis: If flavour, size or colour is chosen before the quantity ladder on every product page, then the PDP is easier to use because shoppers learn 1 consistent pattern across the catalogue.

signal.check: Some product pages show the quantity ladder before the variant selector, or the order is inconsistent across products.

risk.note: A layout change handled with 07-LPG.

prerequisites: Products with both a variant selector and a quantity ladder
steps: Audit product pages for the current order of variant selector and quantity ladder.
Standardise every sibling product to show variant first, then quantity.
Hand the layout change to 07-LPG.

test.method: Compare cart-add rate before and after reordering the selectors.

title: Show the per-unit or per-day price next to the total on every tier
hypothesis: If every tier shows its per-unit, per-serving or per-day price next to the total, then trust and conversion improve because a large total is broken into a number the buyer can compare without hiding it.

signal.check: A quantity break or bundle tier shows only the total price, with no per-unit or per-day figure next to it.

risk.note: A copy and layout change only.

prerequisites: Units or days of use per tier
steps: Compute per-unit, per-serving or per-day price for each tier.
Add it next to the total on every tier, never instead of the total.
Divide by units or days of actual use, never an arbitrary number.

test.method: Compare conversion before and after adding the per-unit figure.

title: Make every ladder tier, including the deepest, clear the contribution target
hypothesis: If every tier, including the deepest, is checked against the contribution target after discount, gifts and freight, then the ladder never quietly loses money on its most popular or biggest tier.

signal.check: Ladder tiers were priced without a per-tier contribution check that includes freight and gift costs.

risk.note: A calculation check before or after launch.

prerequisites: Contribution target (CP_target) from the offer economics baseline
steps: Compute contribution per tier, including gift cost and freight, for every tier.
Compare each to the contribution target.
If the deepest tier fails, cut its savings or gifts, never the shallow tiers.
Recheck after any price or freight change.

test.method: Recompute contribution per tier after launch using real order data.
test.read_point: After 1 order cycle, and after any freight or price change

title: Read take rate per tier after launch and retune the ladder
hypothesis: If we read take rate by tier after at least 1 repeat cycle and retune prices or quantities, then AOV keeps improving because a ladder where most buyers pick tier 1 is not working as designed.

signal.check: A ladder has been live for at least 1 repeat cycle but nobody has checked take rate by tier.

risk.note: A review step; retuning stays within existing unit economics.

prerequisites: Orders by tier for at least 1 repeat cycle
steps: Pull orders by tier for the last repeat cycle.
If most buyers pick the smallest tier, the ladder is not working.
Retune quantities, prices or savings within the contribution target.
Re-check take rate after the retune.

test.method: Compare take rate distribution across tiers before and after retuning.

title: Consider subscription plus a gift instead of a bundle ladder
hypothesis: If a replenishment product uses subscription opt-in plus a free gift instead of a quantity ladder, then repeat purchase can improve because some products fit subscription and a gift better than a multi-pack.

signal.check: A replenishment product runs no bundle and no subscription option, or runs a bundle ladder with weak take rate on a product that repeats predictably.

risk.note: An alternative structure, not a required replacement.

prerequisites: A replenishment product with a real repeat cycle
steps: Confirm the product replenishes on a predictable cycle.
Build a subscription option with a useful, low-cost gift instead of a quantity ladder.
Test it against the existing bundle ladder if one is live.

test.method: Compare take rate and 90-day repeat rate between the subscription-plus-gift offer and the bundle ladder.

title: Layer a bundle with a kit, subscription unlock, or scaling gift
hypothesis: If a costed bundle is layered with a starter kit, a subscription unlock, or a scaling gift, then the offer converts better than any single mechanic alone, as long as the presentation stays simple.
does_not_apply_when: The layered offer becomes confusing to read in the buy box; simplify before adding another layer

signal.check: The bundle ladder is costed and live but carries no kit, subscription unlock or scaling gift on top of it.

risk.note: Too many layers can confuse the buy box; check readability after adding a layer.

prerequisites: A costed bundle ladder already in place
steps: Confirm the ladder is costed and clears its contribution target.
Add 1 layer: a starter kit, a subscription unlock, or a scaling gift.
Check the buy box is still legible in 2 to 3 seconds after the layer is added.
Cost the combined offer before launch.

test.method: Compare AOV and take rate before and after the new layer is added.

title: Choose gifts that help the buyer use the core product, not swag
hypothesis: If gifts with purchase are tools that help use the core product (a frother, a dosing tool, a sample) instead of swag, then take rate improves because the gift adds real usefulness the buyer will notice.

signal.check: The current gift with purchase is a tote bag, sticker or other generic item unrelated to using the core product.

risk.note: Swapping gift items is reversible.

prerequisites: Landed cost and sourcing for a usage-relevant gift
steps: List what helps the buyer use the core product (a tool, a sample, a dosing aid).
Exclude swag and any gift with no use tied to the product.
Source the gift and check its landed cost and box fit.
Replace any current swag gift with the usage-relevant one.

test.method: Compare gift take rate and repeat purchase before and after swapping the gift.

title: Prefer a low-landed-cost gift over an equivalent-cost cash discount
hypothesis: If a gift costing under 5 to 10 dollars in landed cost replaces an equal-percent cash discount, then margin holds because the gift costs the brand less than the cash it replaces while still reading as a real bonus.

signal.check: A cash discount is running on a product where a low-landed-cost SKU or sample already exists in the catalogue or from a supplier.

risk.note: Requires more than 1 SKU or a sample format to work.

prerequisites: Landed cost per SKU
A low-cost SKU or sample available to give away
steps: List SKUs or samples with landed cost under about 5 to 10 dollars.
Compare the cost of gifting one against the equal-percent cash discount it would replace.
Swap the cash discount for the gift where the gift costs less.
Track take rate to confirm buyers still respond.

test.method: Compare contribution per order between the cash-discount and gift versions.

title: Scale the gift with units and place it on the tier you want to sell
hypothesis: If more or better gifts are attached to higher tiers, then take rate on the target tier rises because the gift makes the jump to that tier feel like the bigger win.

signal.check: The same gift is given at every tier, so there is no extra reason to pick a bigger tier over the smallest one.

risk.note: Gift cost must stay inside each tier's contribution target.

prerequisites: Contribution check (F10) per tier including gift cost
steps: Pick the tier the brand most wants to sell.
Give that tier and above a bigger or better gift than the tiers below it.
Confirm gift cost is included inside each tier's contribution check.
Track take rate by tier after the change.

test.method: Compare take rate by tier before and after scaling the gift.

title: Never gift more of the same product the customer just bought
hypothesis: If gifts are never more units of the same product just purchased, then perceived value holds because giving away the same item devalues the price the customer just paid for it.

signal.check: A promotion or gift roadmap gives away extra units of the exact product the customer bought, framed as a gift rather than a bundle tier.

risk.note: A rule to apply when designing gift roadmaps and welcome kits.

prerequisites: Current gift roadmap or welcome kit contents
steps: Review the gift roadmap for any gift that is the same product just purchased.
Replace it with a different, usage-relevant item.
If a free extra unit is intended as a bundle tier, cost and label it as a tier, not a gift.

test.method: Not a live test; a design check applied before any gift roadmap ships.
test.read_point: Before the gift roadmap or welcome kit launches

title: Announce the gift at every step and require a claim action
hypothesis: If the gift is shown on the PDP, in onboarding and in the billing reminder, with a click to claim, then it actually influences purchase because a hidden surprise gift only reaches people who were staying anyway.

signal.check: A gift with purchase exists but is not shown on the PDP, in onboarding, or in any reminder before it ships.

risk.note: A visibility and messaging change, coordinated with 14-EML.

prerequisites: A defined gift with a landed cost and delivery point
steps: Add the gift to the PDP before purchase.
Mention it again in onboarding and the billing reminder.
Add a click-to-claim step where the platform allows it.
Check the gift is never a silent, unannounced surprise.

test.method: Compare take rate and awareness of the gift before and after making it visible at every step.

title: Test any order-2 gift's payback before scaling it to every subscriber
hypothesis: If an order-2 gift is tested for payback against churn by order number before it is rolled out to everyone, then margin holds because an untargeted order-2 gift usually costs more than the retention it buys.

signal.check: An order-2 or early-order gift is planned or running for every subscriber with no payback check against churn by order number.

risk.note: Untargeted gifts at scale can cost more than the retention lift they produce.

prerequisites: Churn rate by order number
Gift landed cost
steps: Get churn by order number and the gift's landed cost.
Compute incremental value (orders with gift minus orders without, times gross margin) against gift spend.
Only keep the gift if incremental value exceeds gift spend.
If it fails, move the gift to a targeted save or the acquisition promise instead.

test.method: Run the gift against a holdout of subscribers who do not receive it.
test.read_point: After the cohort reaches order 3 or 90 days

title: Make bonuses practical tools or how-to content, not more reading
hypothesis: If bonuses are short how-to videos, dosing guides or checklists instead of long guides, then they get used and help retention because a tool or checklist removes effort while a long course adds it.

signal.check: The current bonus is a long ebook, course or guide with no short tool or checklist version.

risk.note: Content creation cost only; near-zero incremental delivery cost.

prerequisites: The specific reason buyers think they will fail to use the product well
steps: Name the specific reason buyers think they will fail to get the result.
Build a short tool, checklist or how-to video that removes that exact friction.
Replace or add it alongside any long guide currently offered.
Confirm the bonus is actually delivered and used, not just sent.

test.method: Compare bonus usage and repeat purchase between the short-tool bonus and the long-guide bonus.

title: State bonus and kit values only at real, sellable prices
hypothesis: If every stated bonus or kit value is a price the item is actually sold at, then trust and legal risk both hold because no stacked value claim can be shown to be invented.

signal.check: A kit or bundle page states a total bonus value that includes items never sold at that price on their own.

risk.note: An inflated bonus value is a reference-value and dark-pattern risk in several markets.

prerequisites: A real selling price for every item included in a stated bonus value
steps: List every bonus or kit item with a stated value.
Confirm each one is sold at that price somewhere, or remove the stated value.
Flag any remaining reference-value claim for a web check by country.

test.method: Not a live test; a compliance audit of every stated value.

title: Give each gift in a 2-gift tier a distinct job instead of a choice
hypothesis: If a tier or kit with 2 gift items gives each one a clear, distinct job instead of asking the buyer to choose one, then conversion holds because a deferred choice at checkout is often a decision not made.

signal.check: A tier or kit asks the buyer to pick 1 of 2 gift options at checkout or on the PDP.

risk.note: A layout and copy change; test before assuming it wins.

prerequisites: A tier or kit currently offering a choice between 2 gifts
steps: Identify any tier or kit asking buyers to choose between 2 gifts.
Give each gift a distinct job (for example 1 for setup, 1 for daily use) instead of a choice.
Include both gifts automatically rather than asking the buyer to pick.
Test the automatic version against the choice version.

test.method: A/B test giving both gifts automatically against asking the buyer to choose one.

title: Set cart thresholds from the order-value distribution, not the average
hypothesis: If a spend or free-shipping threshold is set just above a real peak in the order-value distribution instead of at the mean AOV, then it moves a real band of orders because a threshold near the mean only gives away shipping to buyers already above it.

signal.check: A cart threshold is set at or near the reported mean AOV, with no plot of the order-value distribution behind it.

risk.note: A data analysis step before setting or moving a threshold.

prerequisites: Order-level order values for 90 to 180 days
steps: Export order-level order values for 90 to 180 days.
Plot the count of orders by value band and find the peaks.
With 2 peaks, aim a threshold just above each one.
With 1 peak, aim to move the core group 1 step up.
Never set the threshold at the mean or between peaks.
Re-plot after any price, bundle or threshold change.

test.method: Compare the share of orders that move above the new threshold against the share already above it.

title: Verify a free-shipping threshold pays for itself before keeping it
hypothesis: If we compute the extra contribution from orders that cross the threshold against the shipping given away to orders already above it, then we know whether the free-shipping threshold is a real lever or a weak, money-losing one.

signal.check: A free-shipping threshold is live with no check of how many orders it actually moved versus how many got free shipping for nothing.

risk.note: A weak threshold on a low-AOV item can lose more than paid shipping would have cost.

prerequisites: Order-level data before and after the threshold launched, or a holdout
steps: Measure the share of orders already above the threshold before it launched.
Measure the share of orders that moved from below to above the threshold after launch.
Compute contribution at the threshold including the now-unpaid shipping.
Keep the threshold only if moved-order gains exceed given-away shipping cost.

test.method: Run the check quarterly, or immediately after a price or shipping-cost change.
test.read_point: 30 to 90 days after launch, then quarterly

title: Unlock a product, sample or gift at the cart threshold, not only shipping
hypothesis: If the cart threshold unlocks a product, sample or gift instead of only free shipping, then more orders cross it because a tangible unlock is a stronger pull than shipping alone.

signal.check: The only thing a cart threshold unlocks is free shipping, with no product or sample unlock tested.

risk.note: Layout work sits with 07-LPG; economics of the unlocked item are costed here.

prerequisites: A low-cost product or sample suitable for a threshold unlock
steps: Pick a low-cost product or sample to unlock at the threshold.
Cost the unlock using the tier contribution formula.
Add a progress indicator in the cart showing the unlock.
Consider chaining unlocks: free shipping first, then the product unlock.

test.method: Compare cart-to-checkout conversion and AOV before and after the unlock is added.

title: Frame cart offers as the more you add, the more you save, and check it raises contribution
hypothesis: If cart offers are framed as a rising saving tied to basket size (10% off over $120, 3 items 15% off) and checked against contribution, then AOV rises without a margin loss because the saving is confirmed to pay for itself.

signal.check: A cart-level discount exists with no check that the resulting bigger basket actually raises contribution per order.

risk.note: A framing and verification step.

prerequisites: Order value distribution
Contribution model
steps: Frame the cart offer as a rising saving tied to basket size.
Compute contribution per order at the new, bigger basket size.
Confirm contribution rises, not just revenue.
Adjust the threshold or saving if contribution does not rise.

test.method: Compare contribution per order before and after the cart offer launches.

title: Trigger cart offers on adding an item, not unconditionally
hypothesis: If a cart offer (free shipping, an upgrade to subscribe-and-save) only appears after the buyer adds a specific item, then it converts better because a triggered offer beats an unconditional one shown to everyone.

signal.check: A cart-level offer is shown to everyone regardless of what is in the cart, with no add-triggered version tested.

risk.note: The trigger item must clear the upsell-scoring formula before it is chosen.

prerequisites: Ability to trigger a cart message on adding a specific item
The trigger item scored by incremental contribution
steps: Score candidate trigger items by incremental contribution per exposed order.
Set the cart offer to appear only after the buyer adds that item.
Verify UI: confirm the cart or checkout platform can trigger on item add.
Compare the triggered version against the unconditional one.

test.method: A/B test the add-triggered cart offer against the unconditional version.

title: Keep 1 relevant offer per cart slot, legible in 2 to 3 seconds
hypothesis: If each cart slot shows only 1 relevant, quickly legible offer instead of 3 competing ones, then cart-to-checkout conversion improves because too many offers cause decision fatigue.

signal.check: The cart drawer shows more than 1 offer or cross-sell in the same slot, or an offer on an irrelevant item.

risk.note: A layout simplification, handled with 07-LPG.

prerequisites: Current cart drawer layout and its offer slots
steps: Audit the cart drawer for how many offers appear per slot.
Cut down to 1 offer per slot, chosen for relevance to the cart's contents.
Keep the copy simple enough to read in 2 to 3 seconds.
Use a flat discount on the added item as the default copy pattern.

test.method: Compare cart-to-checkout conversion before and after simplifying to 1 offer per slot.

title: Score every upsell and cross-sell by incremental contribution, not take rate
hypothesis: If every upsell or cross-sell candidate is ranked by take rate times added order value times gross margin of the added item, then upsell slots make more money because the ranking is not skewed by take rate or AOV lift alone.

signal.check: Upsell and cross-sell candidates are ranked by take rate or AOV lift alone, with no incremental-contribution formula applied.

risk.note: A ranking calculation; no live change on its own.

prerequisites: Take rate, added order value and gross margin percent for each upsell candidate
steps: Get take rate, added order value and gross margin percent for each candidate.
Compute take rate times added value times gross margin percent for each.
Rank candidates by this incremental contribution figure.
Fill upsell slots with the top-ranked candidates, not the highest take rate.

test.method: Not a live test on its own; feed the ranking into the placement test below.
test.read_point: Before choosing which candidates to place

title: Measure upsell lift against a holdout, not against takers alone
hypothesis: If upsell lift is measured against a holdout group that never sees the offer, then the true incremental value is known because takers self-select and their AOV overstates the real lift.

signal.check: Upsell performance is reported as the AOV or revenue among people who took the upsell, with no holdout comparison.

risk.note: A measurement change coordinated with 09-CRO.

prerequisites: Ability to hold out a control group from seeing the upsell offer
steps: Set aside a holdout group that never sees the upsell offer.
Compare average order value and gross profit between the offered group and the holdout.
Use this holdout-based lift, not the takers' raw AOV, in every upsell report.

test.method: Run the holdout comparison for at least 1 full read cycle per 09-CRO's sample size.

title: Place upsell offers by friction level: cart, checkout, then post-purchase
hypothesis: If in-cart offers are threshold unlocks, checkout offers are low-friction add-ons only, and post-purchase one-click offers carry full products, then take rate and contribution both improve because each slot matches its natural friction level.
does_not_apply_when: The checkout platform does not support one-click post-purchase upsells (verify UI)

signal.check: A full product is being sold at checkout, or a low-friction add-on is placed post-purchase instead of at checkout.

expected_effect.size: 5% to 15% in-cart, 35% to 40% post-purchase one-click (source's own experience, not a benchmark)

risk.note: Placement changes are reversible; verify platform support for one-click post-purchase.

prerequisites: Checkout platform supports the intended add-on or one-click flow (verify UI)
steps: Move threshold-unlock offers to the cart, not checkout or post-purchase.
Keep checkout to a single low-friction add-on (shipping protection, expedited delivery).
Move full-product offers to a post-purchase one-click page.
Verify UI support for one-click post-purchase before building it.

test.method: Compare take rate and incremental contribution by placement after moving offers.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks of traffic per placement

title: Anchor post-purchase upsells high, then offer a cheaper down-sell
hypothesis: If the first post-purchase offer is priced high and a cheaper down-sell follows only if declined, then revenue per visitor improves because leading with the cheapest item anchors low and makes everything after look expensive.

signal.check: The post-purchase upsell chain leads with its cheapest item instead of its highest-priced one.

expected_effect.size: RPV target 10% to 15% of AOV (source's own benchmark, not this brand's)

risk.note: Requires a real timer only if the chain is time-limited; never a fake one.

prerequisites: A post-purchase one-click upsell page that supports a chain of offers
steps: Reorder the post-purchase chain to lead with the highest-priced offer.
Set a cheaper down-sell to appear only if the first offer is declined.
Set a mid-priced offer to appear if the down-sell is taken.
Only use a countdown on the chain if the time limit is real.

test.method: Compare revenue per visitor from the reordered chain against the old order.

title: Review checkout add-ons like shipping protection for margin and compliance
hypothesis: If a checkout add-on like shipping protection is reviewed for its real margin and never pre-ticked, then it adds profit safely because the margin is real but pre-selection is a compliance risk in several markets.

signal.check: A checkout add-on exists and is pre-ticked by default, or its take rate and margin have never been reviewed.

expected_effect.size: about 30% take, near 100% margin in the source's own example (not this brand's number)

risk.note: A pre-ticked add-on is a dark-pattern risk in several markets; check before keeping it.

prerequisites: Claim rate and carrier terms for any protection add-on
steps: Confirm the add-on is opt-in, never pre-ticked, at checkout.
Get claim rate and carrier terms to confirm the real margin.
Flag pre-selected checkout add-ons for a web check by country.
Remove or fix any add-on that is pre-ticked.

test.method: Track take rate and gross margin on the add-on after making it opt-in.

title: Use product samples in a later box as cross-sells, not onboarding sales emails
hypothesis: If a sample of a second product ships inside a later subscription box instead of being pitched in an onboarding sales email, then cross-sell take rate improves because the sample doubles as a gift the buyer already trusts.

signal.check: Cross-sell attempts happen through onboarding sales emails with low response, while no product sample has been tried inside a later box.

risk.note: Requires packing coordination; email execution stays with 14-EML.

prerequisites: A second product suitable for a small sample
Packing capacity to add a sample to a later box
steps: Pick a second product to sample.
Place a sample of it inside order 2 or later, framed as a gift.
Follow up briefly in email or the next box, not a hard-sell onboarding email.
Compare cross-sell purchase rate against the prior onboarding-email approach.

test.method: Compare cross-sell take rate between the sample-in-box approach and onboarding email.

title: Feed measured upsell gains into the allowable CAC
hypothesis: If the measured contribution gain from an upsell is added to the allowable CAC, then the paid team can spend more per order profitably because the true per-order contribution now includes the upsell.

signal.check: A holdout-measured upsell gain exists but the allowable CAC or bid targets have not been updated to include it.

risk.note: A calculation update, not a live change.

prerequisites: Holdout-measured upsell contribution gain
steps: Get the holdout-measured incremental contribution per order from the upsell.
Add it to the current allowable CAC.
Hand the new allowable CAC to the paid team in writing.

test.method: Track achieved CPA against the new allowable CAC for 2 weeks after the update.
test.read_point: 2 weeks after the CAC ceiling updates

title: Aim the first order at subscription when cohorts show a large LTV gap
hypothesis: If the brand's own cohorts show subscriber LTV well above one-time LTV at 90 days or 6 months, then optimising the first order for subscription raises long-term profit because one-time buyers rarely convert to subscription later.

signal.check: The brand sells a consumable with repeat use but has never compared subscriber LTV to one-time LTV at 90 days or 6 months.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources report 50% to 3x gaps at 6 to 24 months, but self-selection inflates these

risk.note: A measurement and positioning shift, not a price change.

prerequisites: Cohort LTV by first-order type at 90 days, 6 and 12 months
steps: Pull cohort LTV split by one-time versus subscription first order.
Compare the gap at 90 days, 6 and 12 months.
If the gap is large, redesign the buy box to favour subscription (see later ideas in this group).
If the gap is small or unmeasured, do not assume a source's numbers apply.

test.method: Recompute the LTV gap quarterly using the brand's own cohorts.
test.read_point: Quarterly, and before any subscription buy-box redesign

title: Replace a flat 10 to 15% subscribe-and-save discount with a stronger reason to subscribe
hypothesis: If a flat 10 to 15% subscribe-and-save discount is replaced with a front-loaded discount, a gated kit, or a bulk-tier value stack, then subscription take rate rises because a small flat percent gives no real reason to subscribe today.

signal.check: The only subscription incentive is a flat 10 to 15% discount on 1 SKU, with no kit, gated perk or value stack attached.

risk.note: Which replacement model works is contested between sources; model options before committing.

prerequisites: Contribution margin per order
Cohort retention curve
steps: Confirm the current offer is a flat 10 to 15% subscribe-and-save with nothing else attached.
Model 2 to 3 replacement options: front-loaded discount, gated kit, or bulk-tier stack.
Pick the option with the best modelled cohort profit.
Launch and track take rate against the old flat discount.

test.method: Compare subscription take rate before and after replacing the flat discount.
test.read_point: After 1 to 2 months of the new offer

title: Put subscription-only perks on subscription and keep one-time visible but small
hypothesis: If the discount, welcome kit, guarantee and program access sit only on the subscription option while one-time stays visible at full price and small, then subscription take rate rises because the incentive is concentrated on the choice the brand wants.
does_not_apply_when: No test has confirmed one-time demand can absorb losing its own discount

signal.check: One-time and subscription options currently get the same discount or perks, giving no reason to prefer subscription.

risk.note: Removing a one-time discount without testing it first can lose one-time demand.

prerequisites: One-time versus subscription conversion and LTV data
steps: Move the discount, welcome kit, guarantee and program access onto the subscription option only.
Keep the one-time option visible at full price, smaller and recessed in the layout.
Test the change against a holdout of the old, equal-offer layout.
Watch one-time conversion for a drop that outweighs the subscription gain.

test.method: A/B test the gated buy box against the old equal-offer layout.

title: Pre-select subscription among 3 options, 2 of them subscriptions
hypothesis: If the buy box shows 3 options with 2 being subscription plans and 1 pre-selected, then subscription take rate rises because default bias decides most buyers' choice.

signal.check: The buy box defaults to one-time purchase, or shows only 1 subscription option next to 1 one-time option.

risk.note: Pre-selecting a recurring charge is regulated in some markets; disclose price, cadence and cancel terms next to the default.

prerequisites: Verify UI: subscription widget supports a pre-selected default
Web check: pre-selected subscription disclosure rules by country
steps: Add a 2nd subscription plan (for example a longer cadence) next to the existing 1.
Set 1 subscription plan as the pre-selected default.
State price, cadence and cancel terms clearly next to the default.
Keep one-time visible as the 3rd, non-default option.

test.method: Compare subscription take rate before and after the 3-option, pre-selected layout.

title: Front-load the subscription discount and lower the recurring rate
hypothesis: If the first subscription order carries a bigger discount (for example 25 to 30%) and the recurring rate is lower (for example 5 to 10%), then take rate rises while margin is protected, as long as 90-day LTV confirms the front-loaded cohort still pays back.
does_not_apply_when: Churn after order 1 for front-loaded cohorts is unknown; model with a lighter structure first in that case

signal.check: The subscription discount is flat across every order instead of front-loaded, with no LTV read on any front-loaded test.

risk.note: A front-loaded discount can attract buyers who churn right after order 1; watch churn closely.

prerequisites: Cohort survival curve
Gross margin at the net first-order price
steps: Model the front-loaded discount and lower recurring rate with the cohort survival curve.
Confirm first-order margin at the net price is still acceptable.
Launch and track churn after order 1 for the front-loaded cohort.
Compare 90-day LTV of front-loaded cohorts against the current structure.
Choose the profit shape (front-loaded versus back-loaded) that modelled total cohort profit favours.

test.method: Compare 90-day LTV and churn after order 1 between the front-loaded cohort and the prior structure.
test.read_point: 90 days after the front-loaded cohort's first order

title: Set subscription take-rate targets from contribution margin, not an arbitrary number
hypothesis: If subscription take-rate targets come from contribution margin and cohort retention instead of a fixed percent goal, then CAC stays under control because pushing take rate past what margin supports usually raises CAC by pulling in buyers who do not want to subscribe.

signal.check: The team has a fixed take-rate target (like 80% to 90%) with no link to contribution margin or CAC trend.

risk.note: A target-setting change, not a live product change.

prerequisites: Contribution margin per order
Cohort retention curve
CAC trend
steps: Get contribution margin per order and CAC trend over the last few months.
Set the take-rate target from contribution margin, not a fixed percent.
Watch CAC as take rate rises; if it climbs, stop pushing take rate further.
When CAC becomes hard to hit, test a one-time option, a gift with purchase, or a quiz funnel instead.
