test.method: Track CAC against take rate monthly to find the point where CAC starts rising.

title: Gate the best subscription perks on the exact behaviour wanted
hypothesis: If the best rate, kit or program access is stated plainly to require a specific action (a 90-day supply, a ticked subscription box), then take rate of that behaviour rises because buyers understand exactly what they must do to get the perk.

signal.check: A subscription perk (rate, kit, program) is available without a clearly stated condition, or the condition is buried.

risk.note: A copy and layout clarity fix.

prerequisites: A defined perk and the exact behaviour it should be gated on
steps: Pick the behaviour the brand wants (a longer supply, the subscription tick).
State plainly at the point of choice that the perk requires that behaviour.
Remove any wording that lets buyers get the perk without doing it.
Track take rate of the gated behaviour after the change.

test.method: Compare take rate of the gated behaviour before and after the gate is stated plainly.

title: Match subscription cadence and pack size to real use, and let customers adjust it
hypothesis: If subscription cadence and pack size match real usage rate and customers can change frequency easily, then churn from too much product falls because the most common cancel reason is fixed at the source.

signal.check: Cadence is fixed at a default like 30 days regardless of product use rate, and customers cannot easily change frequency.

risk.note: Requires portal support for frequency change; coordinate with 17-CXP.

prerequisites: Servings per pack
Real use rate
Cancel reasons by plan
steps: Get servings per pack and the real use rate for daily-use products.
Offer multiple cadences (for example 3, 5 and 6 weeks), not only 1 default.
Make frequency change easy and visible in the customer portal.
Track 'too much product' as a cancel reason before and after.

test.method: Compare the share of cancels citing too much product before and after cadence options are added.

title: Add a longer or prepaid subscription plan with extra value
hypothesis: If a longer or prepaid plan is added with a deeper discount or bigger kit, then cash comes in sooner and churn falls because prepaid commitment is rewarded and pulls cash forward.

signal.check: Only 1 short cadence plan exists, with no prepaid or longer-term option and its extra value.

risk.note: The prepaid discount must be costed against the churn it saves before setting the depth.

prerequisites: Churn rate by plan length
Cost of the discount or kit at the prepaid tier
steps: Design a longer or prepaid plan (90-day, 6-month or annual).
Attach extra value (a bigger kit, a deeper discount) sized against the churn it should save.
Launch the plan alongside the existing shorter cadence.
Track prepaid uptake and churn by plan length.

test.method: Compare churn and cash timing between prepaid and standard-cadence subscribers.
test.read_point: After 90 days of the prepaid plan being live

title: Design a gift roadmap that lands at high-churn months, shown before purchase
hypothesis: If gifts are placed at the subscription's highest-churn months and announced as an acquisition promise before purchase, then churn falls at those points because buyers already expect and value the reward.

signal.check: No gift roadmap exists, or gifts are placed randomly instead of at the months where churn is highest.

risk.note: Cost each gift inside the tier's contribution before committing.

prerequisites: Churn by order number or month
Landed cost per gift
steps: Pull churn by order number or subscription month.
Place gifts at the 2 to 3 months where churn peaks.
Announce the roadmap on the PDP and in onboarding before purchase.
Cost each gift inside the relevant order's contribution target.

test.method: Compare churn at the targeted months before and after the roadmap ships.
test.read_point: After the cohort passes the targeted months

title: Set a results-timeline promise that matches real evidence for slow-acting products
hypothesis: If onboarding sets a 90 to 120 day results horizon backed by real evidence for slow-acting products, then early cancels fall because buyers stop expecting a result the product cannot deliver that fast.

signal.check: Onboarding or marketing promises results faster than the product's real evidence supports, and cancels cluster around the promised date.

risk.note: The timeline must be supported by real evidence; do not invent a results claim.

prerequisites: Evidence for the product's real results timeline
steps: Get the real evidence for how long results take for this product.
Rewrite onboarding and PDP claims to match that timeline, not a faster one.
Coordinate the rewrite with 14-EML for onboarding emails.
Track cancels around the previously promised date after the change.

test.method: Compare cancel timing before and after the results-horizon message is corrected.
test.read_point: After 1 full cohort passes the new stated horizon

title: Test multiple subscription offers and personas instead of settling on one
hypothesis: If several subscription offers and hooks are tested by persona and tagged at signup, then take rate and LTV both improve because the same product serves several jobs with different conversion and retention.

signal.check: Only 1 subscription offer and hook is live, with no persona tagging at signup and no test of alternate angles.

risk.note: More funnels to maintain; start small before scaling to several personas.

prerequisites: Ability to tag self-selected persona data at popup or post-purchase survey
steps: List distinct personas or jobs the product serves.
Build a separate hook and funnel per persona.
Tag persona data via a popup quiz or post-purchase survey.
Read cohort take rate and LTV by tag, not blended.

test.method: Compare take rate and LTV across persona-tagged cohorts.
test.read_point: After each persona funnel gets enough traffic for a read

title: Size subscription LTV bidding against real cash to carry first-order losses
hypothesis: If subscription acquisition spend is sized against the brand's real cash runway and proven LTGP instead of an LTV target alone, then the brand avoids running out of cash while bidding up subscriber LTV.

signal.check: Acquisition spend is being raised toward a higher LTV ceiling with no check of cash runway to cover the resulting order-1 losses.

risk.note: Bidding up LTV without cash to back it is described in the sources as a fast way to run out of money.

prerequisites: Cash on hand
Proven cohort LTGP and survival curve
steps: Compute LTGP and the CAC ceiling from the brand's own survival curve.
Compute cash runway at the spend level implied by that CAC ceiling.
Cap spend at the level the runway can support, not the LTV ceiling alone.
Recheck monthly as spend and cohorts change.

test.method: Track cash runway monthly against planned spend increases.

title: Check the subscriber cap before pouring more budget into acquisition alone
hypothesis: If we compute the subscriber base cap (new subscribers per month divided by monthly churn) before adding acquisition budget, then spend is better allocated because growth near the cap needs offer, hook and persona work, not just more spend.

signal.check: Acquisition budget keeps rising while the active subscriber base has stopped growing, with no cap calculation done.

risk.note: A calculation and budget-allocation check.

prerequisites: New subscribers per month
Monthly churn rate
steps: Compute the cap: new subscribers per month divided by monthly churn rate.
Compare the current subscriber base to that cap.
If the base is near the cap, shift test budget to offers, hooks and personas.
Keep retention work running regardless of where the base sits versus the cap.

test.method: Recompute the cap and base monthly as acquisition and churn change.

title: Walk the brand's own subscription journey as a customer before redesigning the buy box
hypothesis: If the team buys the product, lives the full subscription journey and calls real subscribers or cancels before redesigning the buy box, then the redesign fixes real friction because it is grounded in what customers actually experience.

signal.check: A subscription buy-box redesign is being planned without anyone on the team having recently gone through signup, delivery, portal and cancel as a customer.

risk.note: A research step before any redesign is committed.

prerequisites: Ability to place a real order and reach real subscribers or recent cancels
steps: Walk the PDP, cart, checkout, confirmation email and first unboxing as a new customer.
Use the subscription for at least 1 cycle, including the portal, skip and cancel flow.
Call a handful of real subscribers or people who cancelled.
Whiteboard what customers like and hate before starting the redesign.

test.method: Not a live test; a qualitative research step done before the redesign begins.
test.read_point: Before any subscription buy-box redesign starts

title: Never let a sitewide sale equal or beat the subscriber discount
hypothesis: If the sitewide sale discount always stays below the subscriber discount, then subscriber cancel-and-rebuy falls because subscribers keep a real reason to stay subscribed during a sale.

signal.check: A sitewide sale is planned or running at a discount equal to or deeper than the subscriber rate.

risk.note: If cancel-and-rebuy is judged acceptable for this brand, this rule can be relaxed deliberately, not by accident.

prerequisites: Current subscriber discount rate
Planned sitewide sale depth
steps: Compare the planned sitewide sale depth to the subscriber discount rate.
If the sale equals or beats it, decide explicitly whether cancel-and-rebuy is acceptable.
If not acceptable, cap the sitewide sale below the subscriber rate, or add a subscriber-only layer.
Track subscriber cancels against the sale period.

test.method: Track subscriber cancels during and after the sale against baseline churn.
test.read_point: During the sale and for 30 days after

title: Build the subscriber offer first, then the public sale
hypothesis: If the subscriber offer for a sale period is designed before the public offer, then subscriber cancel risk falls because the public offer is set to point to what subscribers already get, not the other way round.

signal.check: A sale plan starts with the public discount and only adds a subscriber angle afterward, if at all.

risk.note: A planning-order change.

prerequisites: Subscriber base and their current discount rate
steps: Design the subscriber offer first: deeper on add-ons, extra prepaid months, or a gift for trying a new product.
Set the public offer below the subscriber offer.
Brief ads and email so the public offer points to what subscribers get.
Confirm R91 (public never beats subscriber rate) holds before launch.

test.method: Track subscriber cancels and public sale response together during the sale.
test.read_point: During and 30 days after the sale

title: State the true compounded discount when stacking subscription and sale offers
hypothesis: If the advertised stacked discount is computed the way checkout actually applies it (compounded, not simply added), then trust and margin both hold because a claim like up to 40% off does not overstate a 36% real discount.

signal.check: An advertised total discount adds 2 offers together (like 20% plus 20% equals 40%) without checking whether checkout compounds them instead.

expected_effect.size: the true compounded figure, not the added one

risk.note: An overstated discount claim can be a false-advertising risk.

prerequisites: Verify UI: how the checkout platform combines discounts, additive or compounded
steps: Check whether the checkout platform adds or compounds stacked discounts.
Compute the true stacked percent using that method.
Update every place the stacked discount is advertised to the true figure.
Recheck after any discount-stacking rule change on the platform.

test.method: Place a test order with both discounts applied and confirm the checkout total matches the advertised figure.
test.read_point: Before launch and after any platform update

title: Put a costed, reason-matched discount inside the cancel flow, not upfront
hypothesis: If the cancel flow offers a discount matched to the stated cancel reason and costed against the saved LTGP, then save rate rises without giving away margin on subscribers who would have stayed anyway.

signal.check: The cancel flow shows no discount, or the same discount regardless of the stated cancel reason.

risk.note: Limit repeats so customers do not learn to cancel just to trigger the offer.

prerequisites: Cancel reasons captured in the flow
LTGP of saved subscribers by reason
steps: Map each cancel reason to a matched action: expense gets a discount, too much product gets delay, wrong product gets a swap.
Cost each discount step against the LTGP it would save.
Raise the discount depth only if saved LTGP covers the cost.
Cap how often the same subscriber can use the save offer.

test.method: Compare save rate and saved-subscriber LTGP before and after the reason-matched flow.
test.read_point: After 1 month of the new flow

title: Add a founder video and clear reasons before the cancel offer
hypothesis: If the cancel flow opens with a short founder or brand-voice video and clear reasons before any offer, then save rate rises because context and empathy come before the transaction.

signal.check: The cancel flow jumps straight to an offer or a generic screen with no founder message or reason capture first.

expected_effect.size: from about 5 to 6% toward about 15% in 1 source's client observation (not this brand's number)

risk.note: Verify UI: confirm the subscription platform supports a video splash before the offer step.

prerequisites: A short founder or brand-voice video
Verify UI: platform supports a splash step
steps: Record a short (about 1 minute) founder or brand-voice video for the cancel flow.
Set the flow order: video first, then reasons, then matched actions, then offers.
Confirm cancel is still completable in the same or fewer steps than sign-up.
Track save rate after the reordered flow launches.

test.method: Compare save rate before and after adding the video and reordering the flow.
test.read_point: After 1 month of the new flow

title: Keep cancel findable and completable in as few steps as sign-up
hypothesis: If cancel stays findable in the portal and completable in no more steps than sign-up, then legal risk falls and trust holds because a buried or lengthened cancel path is a dark-pattern risk in several countries.

signal.check: Cancel is hidden behind extra clicks, requires contacting support, or takes more steps than signing up did.

risk.note: Several countries require cancel to be as easy as sign-up; India's 2023 guidelines list subscription traps as a dark pattern.

prerequisites: Current cancel flow step count
Sign-up flow step count for comparison
steps: Count the steps to sign up and the steps to cancel today.
Remove any extra step, required call, or hidden link in the cancel path.
Keep the founder video and matched save offers as content, not obstacles.
Flag for a web check on click-to-cancel rules by selling country.

test.method: Not a live test; a compliance and UX audit of the cancel flow.

title: Cap pause, skip and delay, and treat delay as delayed revenue, not a save
hypothesis: If pause is replaced with a capped, auto-resuming delay (about 30 days) and treated as delayed revenue rather than a save, then chronic skippers get routed to a real offer instead of limbo with low reactivation.

signal.check: The subscription platform offers an open-ended pause with no cap, or a delay is being counted as a successful save.

risk.note: Verify UI: if the platform only supports open-ended pause, cap it in policy even if not in the UI.

prerequisites: Verify UI: platform's pause and delay settings
steps: Rename any auto-resuming pause as a delay.
Cap delay length to about 30 days by default, longer only for large packs.
Stop counting a skip or delay as a successful save in reporting.
Route chronic skippers to a get-it-now bonus or a win-back offer instead.

test.method: Compare reactivation rate for capped delays versus the old open-ended pause.
test.read_point: After 60 days of the capped policy

title: Rotate a win-back offer to cancelled subscribers on a schedule
hypothesis: If a win-back offer rotates to all cancelled subscribers on a regular schedule (weekly to monthly) instead of a single one-off email, then reactivation rate rises because cancelled subscribers keep getting a fresh reason to return.

signal.check: Cancelled subscribers get 1 or 2 win-back emails and then nothing, with no ongoing rotation.

risk.note: Keep the win-back rate invisible to active subscribers.

prerequisites: List of cancelled subscribers
14-EML flow capability
steps: Send an amicable, low-pressure cancel confirmation with no big offer.
Send 1 to 2 short reason-based emails shortly after cancel.
Rotate a new win-back offer to the full cancelled list every 1 to 2 weeks, or a bigger offer 30 to 60 days out.
Judge by click and reactivation rate, and keep the offer invisible to active subscribers.

test.method: Track reactivation rate per rotation and compare to the prior one-off approach.
test.read_point: After each rotation, and again at 90 days

title: Treat subscribers as their own segment with fewer, targeted sends
hypothesis: If subscribers are removed from general campaign sends and given their own lower-volume, purpose-built emails, then cancel rate falls because every send to a subscriber has a stated reason instead of adding noise.

signal.check: Subscribers receive every general marketing campaign at the same volume as one-time buyers, alongside their billing reminders.

expected_effect.size: one A/B test cut cancel rate from 8.6% to 5.8% (1 source's result, not this brand's number)

risk.note: Billing reminders may be legally required in some markets; do not cut them.

prerequisites: Ability to segment subscribers out of general campaign sends
steps: Segment active subscribers out of general campaign email and SMS sends.
Keep billing reminders running; check they meet any auto-renewal notice requirements.
Build a smaller set of subscriber-specific sends, each with a stated purpose.
Track cancel rate after the segmentation change.

test.method: Compare cancel rate before and after segmenting subscribers out of general campaigns.

title: Track and recover failed subscription payments as a revenue lever
hypothesis: If failed subscription payments are tracked and a recovery flow is built, then subscription revenue rises because failed-payment leakage can run 5 to 10% of subscription revenue if left unmanaged.

signal.check: Failed subscription payments are not tracked, or no dunning or recovery flow exists for them.

expected_effect.size: 5% to 10% of subscription revenue is the source's estimate for unmanaged leakage, not this brand's number

risk.note: Build routes through 17-CXP for the recovery flow itself.

prerequisites: Payment failure and recovery data from the subscription platform
steps: Get failed-payment and recovered-revenue figures from the subscription platform.
If none exist, start tracking them now.
Route the dunning and recovery flow build to 17-CXP.
Monitor recovered revenue against the estimated leakage.

test.method: Track failed-payment revenue and recovery rate monthly after the flow launches.

title: Show lost loyalty or reward points in the cancel flow next to the founder video
hypothesis: If the cancel flow shows the loyalty or reward points a customer would lose by leaving, next to the founder video and matched save offers, then save rate may rise because it adds a concrete cost to cancelling for a brand that already runs a points program.
does_not_apply_when: The brand runs no loyalty or points program

signal.check: The brand runs a loyalty or points program but the cancel flow does not show what a cancelling customer would lose.

risk.note: No source models this as its own lever; treat it as an addition to the existing cancel flow, not a replacement.

prerequisites: An active loyalty or points program
Cancel flow that supports adding this element
steps: Confirm the brand runs a loyalty or points program with a real balance per customer.
Show the customer's point balance and what they lose by cancelling, in the cancel flow.
Place it beside the founder video and matched save offers, not instead of them.
Track save rate after the addition.

test.method: A/B test the cancel flow with and without the loyalty-loss message.

title: Cost the guarantee's net contribution before proposing it
hypothesis: If a guarantee's net contribution (orders gained minus refund, return shipping, handling and lost resale value) is computed before proposing it, then a stronger guarantee is only kept when it actually makes more money after real refund cost.

signal.check: A new or stronger guarantee is being proposed with only an assumed order lift and no refund-cost model behind it.

risk.note: A calculation step before any guarantee change ships.

prerequisites: Refund and return rate
Return cost per order
Resale value recovered on returns
steps: Get refund rate, return cost per order and resale value recovered.
Compute net contribution for the current guarantee and the proposed one.
Use a conservative order-lift assumption, not a source's anecdote.
Keep the stronger guarantee only if net contribution actually rises.

test.method: Compare modelled versus actual net contribution after the new guarantee runs.
test.read_point: After 1 to 2 months on the new guarantee

title: Write the guarantee as if not X in Y we will Z
hypothesis: If the guarantee is written as a specific promise (if not X within Y time, we will Z) instead of a generic satisfaction phrase, then conversion rises because buyers see exactly what fear is being removed.

signal.check: The guarantee is worded as a generic phrase like satisfaction guaranteed, with no named fear, timeframe or specific remedy.

risk.note: A copy change; must not overclaim a result the brand cannot support.

prerequisites: The buyer's biggest fear from reviews and support
steps: Name the buyer's biggest fear (fit, durability, taste, results, damage).
Write the guarantee as 'If you do not get X within Y, we will Z.'
Check the X claim is one the brand can substantiate.
Replace any generic 'satisfaction guaranteed' wording with this version.

test.method: Compare conversion on the rewritten guarantee wording against the old version.

title: Decide guarantee length, conditionality, coverage and activation deliberately
hypothesis: If length, conditionality, coverage and activation are each decided on purpose (not defaulted), then the guarantee performs better because vague terms like a full refund with no shipping detail or a clock from order date instead of receipt weaken it.

signal.check: The guarantee's length, conditions, coverage and activation point are not all explicitly stated, or the clock starts from order date instead of receipt.

expected_effect.size: 60 or 90 days often outperform 30 in the sources (their tests, not this brand's)

risk.note: A returns-cost model should back any length beyond a brand's current default.

prerequisites: Returns-cost model (F8) for testing a longer length
steps: State the length explicitly, testing 60 or 90 days if the returns-cost model allows it.
Decide conditionality: unconditional by default, conditional where fulfilment cost is high.
State coverage precisely (say 'product refund' if shipping is not refunded).
Set activation to start on receipt, and spell out the claim method.

test.method: Compare conversion and refund rate before and after clarifying all 4 decisions.
test.read_point: After the sample size 09-CRO sets, or 1 month if not tested

title: Add a second guarantee layer that removes a different risk
hypothesis: If a second guarantee layer (try-before-you-buy, a keep-the-bonus refund, an outsized refund, or a tier-specific durability guarantee) is added on top of the base money-back guarantee, then conversion rises because each layer removes a different risk buyers face.

signal.check: Only a basic money-back guarantee exists, with no second layer addressing a different risk (durability, decision risk, trial risk).

risk.note: The combined worst-case cost of stacked layers must be modelled; delayed capture needs a processor and fraud check.

prerequisites: Worst-case cost model of the combined guarantee layers
steps: Pick a second layer that removes a different risk than the base guarantee.
Model the combined worst-case cost of both layers together.
For delayed capture, check processor support and fraud rate first.
Launch the layer only if combined net contribution still holds.

test.method: Compare conversion and net contribution before and after the second layer is added.

title: Make the guarantee visible near the price and at checkout
hypothesis: If the short version of the guarantee sits near the price and at checkout in plain type, instead of only in a footnote or policy page, then conversion rises because buyers see the risk reversal exactly when they need it.

signal.check: The guarantee is only mentioned in a footer link or a separate policy page, not near the buy box or at checkout.

risk.note: A layout change, coordinated with 07-LPG.

prerequisites: A short-form version of the guarantee text
steps: Write a short-form version of the guarantee (1 line).
Place it under the buy box, near the add-to-cart button.
Repeat it at checkout, near the payment step.
Link the full policy from both short versions.

test.method: Compare conversion before and after moving the guarantee up from the footer.

title: Fix the PDP and reviews first if refund rate is high, before relying on the guarantee
hypothesis: If a high refund rate triggers a PDP and reviews check before any guarantee change, then refund rate falls at the source because a guarantee cannot fix a page that overclaims or a product that disappoints.

signal.check: Refund rate is high and rising, and the response under consideration is only to change the guarantee, not the PDP or product claims.

risk.note: A diagnostic step before any guarantee or product change.

prerequisites: Refund reasons from support or return data
Recent review content
steps: Pull refund reasons from support tickets and return data.
Check the PDP for overclaiming against those reasons.
Check reviews for a pattern of disappointment matching the refund reasons.
Fix the PDP or the product issue before touching the guarantee.
For consumable outcomes, confirm buyers were given a fair use period before judging results.

test.method: Track refund rate for 1 to 2 months after the PDP or product fix.

title: Name the guarantee clearly and on-brand, not with boilerplate
hypothesis: If the guarantee gets a clear, on-brand name instead of a boilerplate label, then it stands out as part of the offer rather than reading as generic legal text.

signal.check: The guarantee is labelled with a generic, boilerplate name like '30 Day Money Back Satisfaction Guarantee' with no brand voice.

risk.note: A naming change only; keep it clear over clever.

prerequisites: The guarantee's core promise already written (from OFF-103)
steps: Draft 2 to 3 name options that are clear and match the brand's voice.
Avoid boilerplate phrasing and avoid shock names that do not fit the brand.
Pick the clearest option, not necessarily the most stylised.
Use the name consistently across the PDP, checkout and policy page.

test.method: Not typically a standalone test; monitor conversion alongside other guarantee changes.

title: Only use all sales final for genuinely non-returnable items, with a true reason
hypothesis: If 'all sales final' is used only for hygiene, customised or perishable items with the true reason stated, then trust and legal compliance both hold because an invented reason for a non-returnable policy is a real risk.

signal.check: An 'all sales final' policy exists on a product without a genuine hygiene, customisation or perishability reason stated.

risk.note: Statutory return rights can override any policy; check them per selling country.

prerequisites: A genuine non-returnable reason (hygiene, customisation, perishability)
steps: Review every product with an 'all sales final' policy.
Confirm each has a real, statable reason for being non-returnable.
Remove the policy from any product with no real reason.
Flag remaining ones for a web check on statutory return rights.

test.method: Not a live test; a policy audit before launch and periodically after.

title: Add a decide-by incentive and reminders to trial and sample offers
hypothesis: If trial and sample offers include a decide-by incentive and follow-up reminders, then activation rises because trials and samples fail through inertia, not only fear, and a nudge closes that gap.

signal.check: A trial or sample offer exists with no decide-by incentive and no reminder sequence to prompt activation or purchase.

expected_effect.size: up to 15% in 1 source's wording test (not this brand's number)

risk.note: Reminder cadence coordinated with 14-EML.

prerequisites: A live trial or sample offer
steps: Add a decide-by date or incentive to the trial or sample offer.
Build a short reminder sequence to prompt activation.
Measure activation and return rate, not just sign-up count.
Sample on the buyer's own stated need where possible.

test.method: Compare activation and conversion rate before and after adding the incentive and reminders.
test.read_point: After the trial or sample window closes for 1 cohort

title: Size guarantee length and conditions for high-ticket items from the returns-cost model
hypothesis: If a high-ticket or considered-purchase guarantee's length and conditions come from the brand's own returns-cost model and statutory rights, then the guarantee protects margin because a broad, low-ticket default is not sized for jewellery-grade or high-cost returns.

signal.check: A high-ticket or jewellery-grade product uses the same broad, short guarantee terms as a low-ticket, one-off item.

risk.note: Guarantee terms interact with statutory rights and resale value on high-ticket items; check both.

prerequisites: Returns-cost model for the high-ticket SKU
Statutory return rights in the selling country
steps: Pull return rate, return cost and resale value for the high-ticket SKU.
Run the guarantee cost formula for 2 to 3 candidate lengths and condition sets.
Check statutory return rights in the selling country as a floor.
Set the final terms from whichever is more generous, the model or the statutory floor.

test.method: Track return rate and net contribution after the sized guarantee ships.

title: Offer store credit as an alternative to a cash refund
hypothesis: If a returning customer is offered store credit (exchange value plus a small top-up) instead of only a cash refund, then cash outflow falls and repeat purchase may rise because the customer stays inside the brand.

signal.check: Returns and exchanges only offer a cash refund, with no store-credit-plus-top-up alternative presented.

risk.note: No source in this playbook models this as a returns lever; verify against the brand's own return data before scaling it.

prerequisites: Ability to issue store credit through the returns process
steps: Add a store-credit option (exchange value plus a small top-up) at the returns step.
Present it alongside, not instead of, the statutory cash-refund right.
Track how many customers choose credit over cash.
Track repeat purchase among customers who took credit.

test.method: Compare repeat purchase and cash refund volume before and after offering the credit option.
test.read_point: After 2 months of the option being live

title: Use scarcity and urgency only when real, enforced and provable
hypothesis: If every scarcity or urgency element (stock count, deadline, claimed bar, reservation timer) is real, enforced and provable from brand data, then trust holds and legal risk falls because a fake countdown or claim loses credibility and breaks several countries' rules.

signal.check: A countdown, stock count, 'X% claimed' bar or reservation timer is live with no live inventory, production limit or real hold behind it.

risk.note: False urgency or scarcity is a dark-pattern risk under several countries' rules, including India's 2023 guidelines.

prerequisites: Live inventory by variant
Production limits
Selling countries confirmed
steps: List every scarcity or urgency element live on any surface.
For each, confirm it is backed by real inventory, a real production limit, or a real time-bound hold.
Remove or fix any element that is not enforced and provable.
Flag every remaining element for a web check by selling country.

test.method: Not a live test; a compliance audit before launch and periodically after.

title: Run limited releases on a fixed, real supply, about monthly at most, with no fake print-run claim
hypothesis: If limited releases run on a fixed, real production run about once a month, sell out visibly, and never claim a fixed run they cannot back, then demand compounds because scarcity stays credible instead of becoming an ignored, oversold claim.
does_not_apply_when: The product is a core SKU that must stay in stock, or is made-to-order with no real cap

signal.check: A limited flavour, colour or design run is planned weekly or more often, or a fixed-run claim is used for a product with no real cap (like a made-to-order item).

risk.note: Over-ordering to avoid selling out defeats the mechanic; under-ordering risks disappointing loyal buyers.

prerequisites: Production or inventory limit that is real and fixed
Confirmation the product is not made-to-order with no cap
steps: Confirm the product has a real, fixed production run or inventory cap.
Never claim a fixed run for a product that can be reordered without limit.
Space limited releases about a month apart, not more often.
Sell out consistently, announce the sell-out, and keep some demand unmet before the next drop.

test.method: Track sell-out speed and repeat interest across successive limited releases.

title: Make the promotion or bonus expire, never the core product
hypothesis: If urgency is always attached to a promotion, bonus, or price rise date rather than the core product's availability, then repeat customers keep trusting the brand because the product itself is never falsely framed as running out.

signal.check: Urgency copy implies the core product itself is running out, when only a promotional wrapper or bonus is time-limited.

risk.note: Never extend a stated deadline once it is published.

prerequisites: A real end date for the promotion or bonus
steps: Set a real end date for the promotion, bonus, or pre-rise price.
Write copy that frames the wrapper or bonus as expiring, not the product.
Never extend the stated deadline once it is live.
Rename the wrapper about every 4 weeks at most if it repeats.

test.method: Not a live test; a copy and policy check applied to every promotion.

title: Set a deadline long enough not to rush, short enough to matter, and test it
hypothesis: If deadline length for a promotion is tested rather than copied from old direct-mail figures, then conversion improves because the right window is brand-specific, not a fixed number from 2009 mail data.

signal.check: A promotion's deadline length was copied from a generic rule of thumb with no test against the brand's own sales-by-hour or sales-by-day pattern.

risk.note: The source figures (7 to 21 days mail, 48 hours email) are stale; treat them as starting points to test.

prerequisites: Sales-by-hour or sales-by-day data from past launches, if available
steps: Pull sales by hour or day from past launches, if available.
Pick 2 candidate deadline lengths to test.
Run each on comparable traffic or in comparable periods.
Keep the length that converts best without shortening so much it feels rushed.

test.method: Compare conversion and revenue concentration across the 2 tested deadline lengths.

title: Keep the core offer evergreen and put urgency on a separate, refreshed flash-deal surface
hypothesis: If bundles and the core offer stay evergreen year-round while urgency lives only on a separate flash-deals surface for overstock, then required efficiency stays low because the main offer is never confused with a rotating discount calendar.

signal.check: The core bundle or offer changes frequently with urgency messaging, instead of staying stable while a separate flash page handles time-limited deals.

risk.note: The flash-deals surface must really refresh and really close, or it becomes another fake-urgency risk.

prerequisites: A separate page or section for flash deals or overstock
steps: Keep the core bundle or subscription offer stable and evergreen.
Build a separate flash-deals page for overstock or clearance only.
Confirm the flash page genuinely refreshes and genuinely closes on schedule.
Do not let flash-deal urgency bleed into the core offer's messaging.

test.method: Track discount share of revenue and price integrity for the core offer over time.

title: Replace a rotating discount calendar with 1 evergreen stacked offer
hypothesis: If a 52-week calendar of rotating percent-off promos is replaced with 1 well-built, stacked evergreen offer, then required ROAS falls because the brand no longer needs to hit a discount-driven efficiency target all year.

signal.check: The brand runs a rotating promo calendar (a different percent off most weeks or months) instead of 1 stable, layered offer.

expected_effect.size: one source's example moved required ROAS from 6x to about 2.9x at the same contribution (not this brand's number)

risk.note: Replacing a promo calendar changes what the marketing team communicates all year; plan the transition.

prerequisites: A costed bundle, subscription unlock or guarantee to layer into the evergreen offer
steps: List the current rotating promo calendar and its average depth.
Build 1 stacked offer combining a bundle, gift, guarantee or subscription unlock.
Cost the stack and confirm required ROAS falls versus the promo calendar.
Retire the rotating calendar and hold the new offer steady.

test.method: Compare required ROAS and discount share of revenue before and after the switch.
test.read_point: After 1 full quarter on the evergreen offer

title: Compute cannibalisation before approving any sale
hypothesis: If displaced full-price revenue, subscriber leakage, pull-forward and refund rate are computed before approving a sale, then the sale only runs when it actually adds incremental contribution instead of just moving revenue around.

signal.check: A sale is planned or approved with no estimate of full-price revenue it would displace, subscriber rebuy leakage, or pull-forward from the following period.

risk.note: A calculation gate before approval, not a live change.

prerequisites: Past sale periods
Subscriber base size
Refund rates in past sales
steps: Estimate the share of the last 30 days' revenue that would have come at full price anyway.
Estimate subscriber rebuy leakage and pull-forward from the next 30 days.
Add expected refund rate at the sale depth.
Approve the sale only if incremental contribution after all of this is above 0.

test.method: Compare the modelled incremental contribution to the actual result after the sale.

title: Set numeric stop rules for every promotion before launch
hypothesis: If every promotion has written stop rules (required ROAS missed for N days, discount share cap, cancel and refund baselines, stock floor) before launch, then losses are capped because the team is not deciding whether to stop while the sale is already underperforming.

signal.check: A promotion is running or planned with no written numeric stop rules and no named owner to enforce them.

risk.note: A planning discipline; enforcement requires a named owner.

prerequisites: The brand's own history to set the required ROAS or CPA threshold
steps: Set a number and owner for: required ROAS or CPA missed for N days.
Set a number and owner for: discount share of revenue above a cap.
Set a number and owner for: subscriber cancels or refund rate above baseline.
Set a number and owner for: stock below the level any scarcity claim states.
Write all 4 into the promotion plan before it launches.

test.method: Check daily or weekly during the promotion against each stop rule.
test.read_point: Daily or weekly during the promotion

title: Treat a seasonal demand dip as a signal to test a new offer
hypothesis: If a predictable seasonal dip (like Q1) is used as a window to test a season-fit offer instead of just accepted, then the dip's impact shrinks because a new offer that fits the season can pull some demand forward.

signal.check: A known seasonal dip is approaching or underway with no offer test planned to address it, only reduced spend.

risk.note: Conversion is naturally suppressed during a dip, so tests need more traffic to read cleanly.

prerequisites: A known seasonal dip pattern from past years' data
steps: Confirm the dip is a known, recurring seasonal pattern.
Design an offer that fits the season instead of the brand's default offer.
Plan for a larger sample size than usual, since conversion is suppressed.
Read the test at 09-CRO's sample size, not on a fixed date.

test.method: Run the season-fit offer during the dip and compare it to the same period last year and to the default offer.
test.read_point: At the end of the seasonal dip period

title: Hold a winning offer 6 to 12 months, then audit it against belief
hypothesis: If a winning offer is held stable for 6 to 12 months instead of tinkered with, then it keeps performing because constant change never lets an offer prove itself, and an audit after 90 to 120 days catches real fatigue without guessing.

signal.check: A working, monetised offer is being changed frequently with no fixed hold period or a scheduled audit.

risk.note: A discipline change, not a live product change.

prerequisites: A currently winning, monetised offer
steps: Set a hold period of 6 to 12 months for the current winning offer.
Test challenger offers only on side funnels during the hold.
At 90 to 120 days, survey buyers on what convinced them and remove unvalued parts.
Check repeat rate by offer as part of the audit.

test.method: Compare offer performance and repeat rate at the 90 to 120 day audit point against the launch baseline.
test.read_point: At 90 to 120 days, then every 6 to 12 months

title: Keep testing offers even though most variants will fail
hypothesis: If the team keeps a backlog of untested offer ideas per SKU and expects most tests to lose or tie, then the brand still finds winners over time because 1 win in a handful of tests can be very profitable.

signal.check: Offer testing stalled after 1 or 2 losing tests, with no backlog of further ideas queued.

risk.note: A planning and expectation-setting change.

prerequisites: A backlog list of candidate offer ideas per SKU
steps: Build and maintain a backlog of offer test ideas per SKU.
Set the expectation that most tests will lose or tie, not just win.
Keep testing on a schedule instead of stopping after 1 or 2 losses.
Track win rate over time, not per test.

test.method: Track cumulative test count and win rate over a quarter.

title: Refresh a fatigued offer in order: creative, copy, wrapper, duration, then price
hypothesis: If a fatigued offer is refreshed in order (creative, then body copy, then headline or wrapper, then duration, then an enhancer, then price last) and stopped at the first step that restores response, then the offer is fixed with the least operational change.

signal.check: Reach and frequency data shows real fatigue, and the planned fix jumps straight to a price or monetisation change.

risk.note: Do not change a working, monetised offer out of boredom; confirm real fatigue with data first.

prerequisites: Reach and frequency data by creative
steps: Confirm fatigue with reach and frequency data, not just time running.
Refresh creative first and test.
If that does not restore response, refresh body copy, then headline or wrapper.
Only after those fail, test duration, then an enhancer, then monetisation and price last.
Stop at the first step that restores response.

test.method: Test each refresh step against the control before moving to the next.
test.read_point: After each refresh step gets a sample-size read

title: Only run a loss-leader SKU when the next purchase route is already built
hypothesis: If a loss-leader SKU is only launched once a bundle upsell, subscription offer, or email flow to route the buyer into the next purchase already exists, then the loss pays back because profit comes from a planned back end, not an unplanned hope.

signal.check: A loss-leader SKU or price is being considered with no bundle upsell, subscription offer, or flow built to capture the next purchase.

risk.note: A loss-leader with no back end built is a straightforward way to lose money on every order.

prerequisites: A built bundle upsell, subscription offer, or 14-EML flow to route the buyer into next
steps: Confirm the next-purchase route (bundle, subscription, or flow) is already built and live.
Cap the loss-leader's loss against modelled cohort contribution from that route.
Launch the loss-leader only once the back end is confirmed working.
Judge the loss-leader on cohort contribution, not on its own order economics.

test.method: Track cohort contribution for loss-leader buyers through the built next-purchase route.

title: Plan offers against the store's real peak-demand calendar, not ad hoc
hypothesis: If offers are planned against a written peak-demand calendar (BFCM, Diwali, EOSS, Republic Day for an India store, or the brand's own equivalents) instead of ad hoc timing, then sale periods land when demand is naturally highest instead of competing with it.

signal.check: Sales and promotions are scheduled ad hoc with no written calendar of the store's known peak-demand dates.

risk.note: The exact festival or peak dates must be checked against the current calendar each year.

prerequisites: The store's selling countries and their known peak-demand periods
steps: List the store's known peak-demand periods (BFCM, regional festivals, EOSS, paydays).
Check the current calendar for exact dates each year.
Build the promotion plan (P16) around these dates instead of ad hoc timing.
Extend the stop-rules and cannibalisation check to every calendar entry.

test.method: Compare sale-period ROAS on calendar-aligned promotions against past ad hoc ones.

title: Run a real first-order offer in the pop-up, not a bare join-us or generic 10%
hypothesis: If the pop-up carries a real first-order offer (mystery framing, a credit, a gift) instead of a bare 'join our community' or plain 10% off, then opt-in and placed-order rate both rise because a weak or generic pop-up converts poorly.
does_not_apply_when: The brand is fixed-offer; test a non-discount hook instead, such as early access or a guide

signal.check: The pop-up shows only a community join message or a plain, unframed 10% off, with no test of a stronger offer.

expected_effect.size: a static 10% off drew about 7% opt-in versus mystery framing of the same 10% about 15% in 1 source's scenario (not this brand's number)

risk.note: Verify UI: confirm the pop-up tool supports the offer format chosen.

prerequisites: Confirmation the brand discounts at all
Verify UI: pop-up tool capability
steps: Confirm whether the brand discounts at all; if not, plan a non-discount hook instead.
Design a real offer: mystery framing, a credit, or a free gift, not a bare message.
Launch the new pop-up offer against the old one.
Read opt-in and placed-order rate, not opt-in alone.

test.method: A/B test the new pop-up offer against the current one on equal traffic.

title: Limit first-order pop-up offers to 4 types: currency off, percent off, free gift, or credit
hypothesis: If pop-up offer testing is limited to currency off, percent off, free gift, or cash back and credit, then test quality improves because giveaways and free guides draw low-quality or low-intent leads for a DTC store.
does_not_apply_when: The purchase is a considered or high-consideration one (jewellery, gifting); a guide or quiz can work there instead

signal.check: The pop-up test roadmap includes a giveaway or a free guide as a lead magnet for a low-consideration DTC product.

risk.note: A test-design filter, not a live change on its own.

prerequisites: The pop-up test roadmap or backlog
steps: Review the pop-up test roadmap for giveaways or free guides.
Replace any giveaway or free guide with 1 of the 4 shortlisted types.
For considered or gifting purchases, keep a guide or quiz as a separate, tested option.

test.method: Not a live test itself; a filter applied when building the pop-up test roadmap.
test.read_point: At each pop-up test planning cycle

title: Test structurally different pop-up offers on equal traffic and judge by profit and LTV
hypothesis: If pop-up offer variants are tested on equal traffic and judged by placed-order rate, gross profit and 90-day LTV instead of opt-ins, then the winning variant is the one that actually makes money, not just the one that collects the most emails.

signal.check: A pop-up test declared a winner based on opt-in count alone, with no placed-order rate, gross profit or LTV read.

expected_effect.size: one source's test: an incumbent free gift at 3.3% placed-order rate lost to a credit offer at 10.7% (its own client's result, not this brand's number)

risk.note: Verify UI: confirm the pop-up tool can split-test equally.

prerequisites: Verify UI: pop-up tool supports a split test
Ability to read gross profit and 90-day LTV by variant
steps: Shortlist structurally different variants (currency off, percent off, gift, credit, mystery framing).
Split equal traffic across variants.
Read opt-ins, placed-order rate, and gross profit after gift or discount cost.
Hold the leaders until 09-CRO's stopping rule and 90-day LTV are both in before declaring a winner.

test.method: Run the multi-variant pop-up test and read profit and LTV, not opt-ins.
test.read_point: After 09-CRO's stopping rule, then again at 90 days

title: Test mystery or exclusive framing against a stated value, do not assume it wins
hypothesis: If mystery or exclusive framing of a discount is tested against stating the value plainly, then the pop-up converts better on the metric that matters because 1 source's own test found the explicit credit figure beat its mystery version.

signal.check: The pop-up uses mystery or exclusive framing with no test against a plainly stated value for the same offer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; results were mixed between sources

risk.note: Verify UI: confirm the pop-up tool supports the reveal format used.

prerequisites: A live mystery-framed or explicit-value pop-up offer to test against
steps: Build a plainly stated version of the current mystery-framed offer.
Run both versions on equal traffic.
Read placed-order rate and gross profit for each, not opt-ins.
Keep whichever wins, and check the revealed value felt worth it either way.

test.method: A/B test the mystery-framed offer against the plainly stated version.

title: Make the pop-up offer match the site's real offer, with 1 true combined number
hypothesis: If the pop-up shows exactly the site's live offer, stacked into 1 true combined number, then trust holds and subscription offers stop looking weak because no separate, conflicting discount undercuts them.

signal.check: The pop-up offers a discount that conflicts with, or undercuts, the site's subscription or bundle offer.

risk.note: A copy and offer-logic fix, coordinated across pop-up and site.

prerequisites: List of every live discount: sitewide, subscription, bundle, welcome code
steps: List every live discount code and offer across the site and pop-up.
Confirm which combine at checkout and whether they add or compound.
Set the pop-up to advertise the true combined number, or 'up to X' only if a further layer really stacks.
Remove any pop-up offer that conflicts with the subscription or bundle offer.

test.method: Place a test order using the pop-up code and confirm the final price matches the advertised number.
test.read_point: Before launch and after any offer change

title: Model the full pop-up chain: opt-ins, revenue, discount cost, and ESP cost
hypothesis: If the whole pop-up chain (new subscribers, revenue per subscriber, discount cost, and ESP tier cost) is modelled together, then the pop-up's real net value is known because a bigger list also means a bigger ESP bill and more discount codes redeemed.

signal.check: Pop-up performance is reported only as opt-in count or opt-in rate, with no revenue, discount cost or ESP cost included.

risk.note: A calculation model, not a live change.

prerequisites: Visitors, opt-in rate, revenue per subscriber, ESP pricing tiers
steps: Get visitors, opt-in rate, and revenue per subscriber.
Get discount code redemption cost from the pop-up offer.
Get the ESP cost at the current list size and the size after growth.
Compute net value: email revenue minus discount cost minus the ESP cost increase.

test.method: Recompute the model monthly as list size and offer terms change.

title: Give exit and abandonment offers by commitment stage, no discount for checkout abandoners
hypothesis: If browsers get a generous offer with urgency, cart abandoners get a small one, and checkout abandoners get only risk reversal or free shipping with no new discount, then margin holds because checkout abandoners were stopped by friction and will likely buy anyway in 2 to 3 days.
does_not_apply_when: The brand already discounts broadly; restate the existing first-order offer instead of adding a deeper one

signal.check: The same discount is offered to browsers, cart abandoners and checkout abandoners regardless of how far they got.

risk.note: Coordinated with 14-EML for the abandoned-flow build.

prerequisites: Ability to segment exit and abandonment offers by commitment stage
steps: Segment offers by stage: browser, cart abandoner, checkout abandoner.
Give browsers a generous offer with real urgency where honest.
Give cart abandoners a small offer.
Give checkout abandoners only risk reversal, a reminder, or free shipping, no new discount.
Test the no-discount checkout-abandoner flow against a holdout if unsure.

test.method: Compare recovered revenue and discount cost across the 3 stages before and after segmenting.
test.read_point: After 1 month of the segmented flows

title: Offer a low-commitment path beside the buy button for considered purchases
hypothesis: If a buying guide, fit quiz, or remind-me capture sits beside the buy button for a considered or gifting purchase, then more not-ready buyers are captured because they get a lower-commitment way to stay engaged instead of leaving.

signal.check: A high-consideration or gifting product page offers only 'add to cart' with no lower-commitment option for buyers who are not ready.

risk.note: A layout addition, not a replacement for the buy button.

prerequisites: A buying guide, fit quiz, or remind-me capture mechanism
steps: Build a buying guide, fit quiz, or remind-me capture for the considered-purchase page.
Place it visibly beside the buy button, not buried below the fold.
Route captured leads into a nurture flow via 14-EML.
For exit intent, ask a 'why not today' question routed by reason (price, fit, timing).

test.method: Compare capture rate and eventual purchase rate with and without the low-commitment path.

title: Run a give-X-get-X referral offer for the repeat-buyer base
hypothesis: If a give-X-get-X referral offer is run for repeat buyers, then acquisition volume rises at a lower cost because existing happy customers bring in buyers the paid channels cannot reach as cheaply.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has no meaningful repeat-buyer base yet to draw referrers from

signal.check: The brand has a repeat-buyer base but runs no give-X-get-X referral offer.

risk.note: No source in this playbook models this; keep it separate from any affiliate or partner program.

prerequisites: A repeat-buyer base
A referral mechanism (code or link) the store platform supports
steps: Confirm the store has a meaningful repeat-buyer base.
Set a give-X-get-X reward for both referrer and new customer.
Launch the referral mechanism through the store platform or an app.
Track referral share of new orders and cost per referred order.

test.method: Compare cost per acquisition and order volume from referral versus paid channels.

title: For a fixed-offer brand, run a presentation audit instead of proposing new discounts
hypothesis: If a fixed-offer brand's whole scope is presentation (stating the offer clearly, showing value, removing friction, adding proof, reinforcing promises) instead of new discounts, then conversion improves within the constraint the owner set.
does_not_apply_when: The owner asks in writing for a new price point, code or gift; only then does this scope expand

signal.check: A fixed-offer brand's improvement plan includes a new discount, code or price change with no written request from the owner.

risk.note: This is a scope constraint from ecomOS itself, applied whenever the owner has fixed the offer.

prerequisites: Confirmation the brand is a fixed-offer brand
steps: Confirm the brand is fixed-offer and the owner has not asked for a price or discount change in writing.
Write the offer in the 5 variables and note which are empty.
Crawl every surface for mismatches and expired promotions.
Run the value-equation and framing passes without proposing any price or code change.
Produce a ranked fix list, cheapest and highest-leverage first.

test.method: Compare conversion before and after the presentation fixes ship, with price held constant.
test.read_point: After 2 to 4 weeks of traffic on the fixed offer

title: Make the offer identical across ad, page, cart, checkout and email
hypothesis: If the ad, landing page, PDP, cart, checkout, confirmation email and support macros all state the same price, saving and terms, then conversion improves because buyers never feel misled between surfaces.

signal.check: A price, saving, or term differs between the ad, page, cart, checkout, email, or support macro, or an expired promotion is still visible somewhere.

risk.note: A congruence audit and fix, run before any launch and after any change.

prerequisites: Access to every live surface: ad, page, cart, checkout, confirmation email, support macros
steps: Screenshot the ad, landing page, PDP, cart, checkout, confirmation email and support macros for 1 offer.
Record the price, saving and terms shown on each.
Fix every mismatch and remove every expired or conflicting promotion.
Repeat this audit before any launch and after any offer change.

test.method: Compare conversion before and after fixing every mismatch found in the audit.

title: Reinforce true promises under the buy box: shipping, cancel-anytime, delivery date
hypothesis: If true promises the brand can already keep (free shipping, cancel or skip anytime, an exact delivery date, the guarantee) are shown under the buy box, then conversion rises because these promises remove buyer doubt at the exact decision point.

signal.check: True facts like free shipping, cancel-anytime, or a real delivery date exist but are not shown near the price or add-to-cart button.

risk.note: Every promise shown must match real fulfilment and policy data; do not overstate.

prerequisites: Dispatch and delivery times by region
Confirmed true policy facts (shipping, cancel terms)
steps: List which promises are true today: free shipping, cancel or skip anytime, delivery date, guarantee.
Check each against real fulfilment data before publishing it.
Add the true promises under the buy box, near the price.
Prefer an exact delivery date over a vague window like '2 weeks'.

test.method: Compare conversion before and after adding the promise block under the buy box.

title: Never copy another brand's claims, counts, or discounts
hypothesis: If every count, percent, and safety claim on the page is the brand's own and true, instead of copied from a competitor's page, then legal and trust risk falls because a copied claim like a customer count or a discount percent belongs to that other brand.

signal.check: Page copy or ad copy includes a customer count, percent-off, or safety claim that was drawn from a competitor's page rather than the brand's own data.

risk.note: A copied or unsubstantiated claim is a legal and trust risk; use competitor pages for layout and mood only.

prerequisites: List of every count, percent, and safety claim currently live
steps: List every count, percent, and safety claim on the page and in ads.
Confirm each is the brand's own, true and current number.
Remove or rewrite any claim traced back to a competitor's page.
Use competitor pages only for layout and mood going forward, per the ecomOS rule.

test.method: Not a live test; a claims audit before launch and periodically after.

title: Cut checkout effort as part of the offer: wallets, guest checkout, fewer fields
hypothesis: If checkout adds express wallets, guest checkout, saved details and fewer required fields, then conversion rises because cutting effort is part of the offer, not a separate project.

signal.check: Checkout forces account creation, has no express wallet options, or asks for more fields than needed to complete the order.

risk.note: Verify UI: confirm wallet and BNPL availability and fees for the selling country before enabling them.

prerequisites: Verify UI: checkout platform supports guest checkout and express wallets
Web check: wallet and BNPL availability and fees per country
steps: Enable guest checkout so account creation is never forced.
Add express wallets and BNPL where available in the selling country.
Cut the checkout form down to the fields actually needed.
Save buyer details for return visits where the platform allows it.

test.method: Compare checkout conversion before and after the friction cuts.

title: Name the offer with the buyer's outcome word, tested on the PDP and in the ad
hypothesis: If the offer or product name uses the buyer's outcome word and the terms buyers actually search for, then conversion and search visibility both improve because a category-only name ('jacket') says less than an outcome word ('warm', 'light fashion jacket').

signal.check: The product or offer name states only the category, with no outcome word for the buyer it targets.

risk.note: Avoid a quantified outcome with a timeframe unless the ad platform allows it (implies a guarantee).

prerequisites: The primary avatar's desired outcome word or phrase
steps: Draft 3 to 5 candidate names using the buyer's outcome word.
For a marketplace listing, use the exact terms buyers search for.
Drop any name stating a quantified outcome with a timeframe unless the ad platform allows it.
Test the candidate name as the PDP title at the same time as the ad headline.

test.method: Run the candidate names as both PDP titles and ad headlines together, not the ad alone.

title: Test a candidate offer name on the PDP at the same time as the ad headline test
hypothesis: If a candidate offer name is tested as the PDP title at the same time it is tested as an ad headline, then the name test is valid because a name buyers never see on the page cannot be proven by an ad test alone.

signal.check: A name test is running only in ad headlines, with the PDP still showing the old or a different name.

risk.note: Coordinate the ad test in 24-DEP with the PDP change.

prerequisites: A candidate name already drafted
Ability to change the PDP title for a test
steps: Pick the candidate name to test.
Update the PDP title to the candidate name for the test period.
Run the same candidate as an ad headline in 24-DEP at the same time.
Read PDP and ad results together, not the ad alone.

test.method: Run the PDP title and ad headline test concurrently on the same candidate name.

title: Build a value comparison against a real alternative on the PDP before the price
hypothesis: If the PDP shows a per-unit or per-day cost comparison against a real alternative the buyer already spends on, placed before the price appears, then conversion rises because the price reads as reasonable next to a real substitute.

signal.check: The PDP states a price with no comparison to a real alternative the buyer already pays for, or the comparison only appears in ad copy.

risk.note: Every comparison must be substantiated with real alternative costs; do not use a compounding-calculator trick or a false close.

prerequisites: Real costs for a genuine alternative the buyer already spends on
steps: Find a real alternative the buyer already spends money on for the same problem.
Get its real cost, stated first, higher-priced alternatives before cheaper ones.
Divide by the actual period of use, never an arbitrary unit.
Place the comparison on the PDP before the price appears.

test.method: Compare conversion before and after adding the value comparison to the PDP.

title: Match the offer claim to the buyer's awareness stage
hypothesis: If the headline claim changes by awareness stage (problem aware, solution aware, product aware) for the same product, then conversion improves because each stage needs a different entry point into the same offer.

signal.check: The same headline claim is shown to all traffic regardless of stated or inferred awareness stage.

risk.note: Requires stage research from 02-AVT to segment traffic or messaging.

prerequisites: Awareness-stage research from 02-AVT
steps: Pull awareness-stage research for the product's key audiences.
Write a distinct headline claim for problem-aware, solution-aware, and product-aware traffic.
Match each claim to the ad or landing page serving that audience.
Carry the same claim from ad to page for each stage.

test.method: Compare conversion by stage-matched landing page against a single generic page.

title: Test offer structure before depth, one variable at a time, on equal traffic
hypothesis: If offer tests change 1 structural variable at a time on equal, message-matched traffic before testing depth, then test results are trustworthy because a clean read needs 1 change, not several at once.

signal.check: An offer test changes more than 1 variable at once, or traffic and landing pages are not equally matched across cells.

risk.note: A test-design discipline; sample size and stopping rules come from 09-CRO.

prerequisites: 09-CRO's sample size and stopping rule for the test
steps: Write the single structural variable being tested, not depth.
Build dedicated, message-matched landing pages per cell.
Split traffic equally across cells.
Get sample size, duration and stopping rule from 09-CRO before launching.

test.method: Run the single-variable test to 09-CRO's stopping rule before reading results.

title: Preselect the test metric before running an offer test
hypothesis: If contribution per visitor, then gross profit after gift or discount cost, then LTV at the repeat-cycle window are chosen as the read metrics before an offer test launches, then the team cannot shift the goalposts once results come in.

signal.check: An offer test is launched with no written metric or with the metric decided only after results start coming in.

risk.note: A discipline step; write which costs count in net profit before launch.

prerequisites: Agreement on which costs count in 'net profit' for this test
steps: Write which costs count in net profit for this test (gift cost, discount cost, returns).
Set contribution per visitor as the primary purchase-test metric.
Set gross profit after gift or discount cost as the secondary read.
Set LTV at the repeat-cycle window as the final read before declaring a lasting winner.

test.method: Not a live test itself; a metric-selection step done before every offer test.

title: Hold creative and landing page constant when testing an offer change to attribute the lift
hypothesis: If ad creative and the landing page stay the same while only the offer changes, then any lift can be credited to the offer alone, because changing both offer and creative at once cannot say which one caused the result.
does_not_apply_when: The test is deliberately hunting for a new creative-and-offer combination, not attributing a single cause

signal.check: An offer test also changed the ad creative or landing page at the same time, with no way to attribute the result to either.

risk.note: A test-design rule; coordinated with 09-CRO.

prerequisites: Ability to hold creative and landing page fixed across test cells
steps: Decide whether the goal is to isolate the offer's effect or to find a new combination.
If isolating, hold creative and landing page fixed across all cells.
Change only the offer variable between cells.
State in the test record which mode (isolate or combination-hunt) was used.

test.method: Run the isolated test and confirm only the offer varied across cells.

title: Start by testing 1 offer element unless a full overhaul is the hypothesis
hypothesis: If offer tests default to changing 1 element (unit price display, variant order, a gift tier) instead of overhauling everything at once, then each test result is easier to read and reuse because the change is small and attributable.

signal.check: Every offer test proposed is a full overhaul rather than a single-element change, with no stated reason a full overhaul is needed.

risk.note: A test-scoping rule.

prerequisites: A test backlog to draw single-element ideas from
steps: Check whether the test hypothesis truly requires a full offer overhaul.
If not, scope the test down to 1 element (price display, variant order, a gift tier).
Run the single-element test before considering a bigger overhaul.
Reserve full overhaul tests for cases with a clear, stated reason.

test.method: Run the single-element test to 09-CRO's stopping rule.

title: Keep a backlog of untested offer ideas; expect most tests to lose or tie
hypothesis: If the team keeps a running backlog of offer ideas and expects most individual tests to lose or tie, then testing continues productively because the payoff comes from the occasional big win, not from every test succeeding.

signal.check: There is no written backlog of offer test ideas, or testing has stopped after a string of losing or tied results.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source's experience puts offer-test response swings between 10% and 900% (a claim, not a benchmark)

risk.note: A planning discipline, distinct from the sequencing rule in structure-before-depth.

prerequisites: A place to log and prioritise offer test ideas
steps: Set up a running backlog of offer test ideas, tagged by SKU.
Set the expectation with the team that most tests will lose or tie.
Keep a steady testing cadence rather than stopping after losses.
Review the backlog and win rate on a fixed schedule.

test.method: Track cumulative tests run and win rate against the backlog over a quarter.

title: Re-test an offer after any change in traffic source or creative
hypothesis: If a previously tested offer is re-tested after a meaningful change in traffic source or creative, then the offer's read stays valid because a new audience shifts AOV and conversion enough to change the answer.

signal.check: The current offer's winning test result is more than a few months old, and traffic source or lead creative has changed meaningfully since then.

risk.note: A scheduling discipline.

prerequisites: A log of when each live offer was last tested and against what traffic
steps: Log the traffic source and creative in place when each offer was last tested.
Watch for a meaningful shift in traffic source or lead creative.
Re-run the offer test when a meaningful shift happens.
Update the offer record with the new result.

test.method: Re-run the same offer test structure against the new traffic or creative mix.
test.read_point: After the sample size 09-CRO sets, following the shift

title: Convert every USD benchmark to the brand's own currency before using it
hypothesis: If every USD threshold or rule of thumb (the dollar-versus-percent rule, the 250 screen, a $25 credit figure) is converted to the brand's own currency and price level before use, then offer decisions stay correct because none of these thresholds were tested outside USD.
does_not_apply_when: The brand already sells in USD at similar price points to the source

signal.check: A USD-based threshold or example figure from a playbook or benchmark is being applied directly, with no currency conversion.

risk.note: A calculation check before applying any USD-based rule of thumb.

prerequisites: The brand's selling currency and typical price points
steps: List every USD threshold or example figure about to be used in an offer decision.
Convert each to the brand's own currency at current rates.
Check whether the underlying price level (not just the exchange rate) still makes the rule sensible.
Flag any converted rule that has never been tested outside USD as unproven for this market.

test.method: Not a live test; a conversion check applied before using any USD-based threshold.
test.read_point: Before every use of a USD-based threshold
